choices: Fault domains — spread instances across the 3 fault domains inside one AD to survive a rack-level failure, and availability domains to survive an AD-level failure
Compartments — isolate workloads with policies so a power event cannot cross a policy boundary
VCN route tables — route database traffic to a backup table when the primary fails
Object Storage buckets — replicate data across buckets, which are isolated power zones
scenarios.hint: OCI has two levels of isolation: one is a set of fault domains sharing a datacenter, the other is an independent datacenter entirely.
scenarios.prompt: Which OCI construct maps to 'different power/cooling/network' isolation, and how would you use it?
scenarios.situation: A startup runs its database primary on one rack and the replica on another rack in the same building. A power bus failure takes down the whole building. The CTO says: 'In OCI, how would we have isolated the two failures — hardware and power?'
scenarios.title: The two-failure scenario
scenarios.why: An availability domain is one or more datacenters with independent power, cooling, and networking — an AD-level failure is contained. Within an AD, three fault domains group racks on different hardware, so a rack failure affects only one fault domain. The pattern: replicate across ADs for site resilience, and across fault domains inside an AD for hardware resilience.

choices: Fault domains protect against rack-level failure inside one AD, but not a full region outage — cross-region replication or a multi-AD region is needed for regional DR
Fault domains require 3 ADs to function; with one AD they silently do nothing
A single-AD region cannot run compute instances, only storage
Multi-AD HA is impossible in OCI; every design must be single-AD
scenarios.hint: Ask: what is the blast radius of a fault domain versus a region?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this design?
scenarios.situation: A team wants multi-AD high availability for their order system. They pick a region that has only one availability domain and deploy 'primary in fault domain 1, standby in fault domain 2'. Their DR test then kills the whole region.
scenarios.title: The single-AD region bet
scenarios.why: Fault domains are intra-AD resilience (independent racks, shared datacenter infrastructure), while regions are independent geographies. Some OCI regions have 1 AD and some have 3. Surviving a region-level event requires a second region (e.g., async replication to a paired region), not more fault domains. Match the failure scope to the isolation construct.

choices: Dedicated Region — a full OCI region operated by Oracle inside the customer's own datacenter, meeting residency and on-premises requirements
A second public region — data residency is satisfied by any EU region
Object Storage Archive tier — archived data is exempt from residency law
IAM compartments — policies can pin data to a country
scenarios.hint: Which OCI option literally puts an entire region inside the customer's building?
scenarios.situation: A European bank must keep customer data inside its own country and needs cloud services behind its firewall for low-latency trading. Public OCI regions don't satisfy legal.
scenarios.title: The data-residency request
scenarios.why: OCI's distributed cloud includes Dedicated Region (a complete OCI region in the customer's datacenter), Oracle Alloy (partners run their own cloud), and Roving Edge for disconnected edge sites. Dedicated Region is the answer for strict residency plus cloud services on-premises; a public region in the same country may satisfy residency but not the behind-the-firewall requirement.

choices: The home region cannot be changed after tenancy creation — IAM resources live in the home region; subscribe to additional regions for workloads instead
The home region can be moved once per year via a support ticket
Changing the home region is automatic when the billing address changes
The home region follows the first VCN created, not the tenancy
scenarios.hint: Which tenancy-level construct is permanently anchored where the tenancy was born?
scenarios.situation: A new tenancy is created with home region us-ashburn-1. Six months later, compliance requires IAM changes to be administered from the EU. The admin tries to 'move' the home region to eu-frankfurt-1.
scenarios.title: The home region lock-in
scenarios.why: The home region is chosen at signup and is immutable: it hosts the tenancy's IAM definitions. You can subscribe to other regions for compute, storage, and networking workloads, but IAM (users, groups, compartments, policies) is anchored to the home region. Choose it deliberately at signup.

choices: A realm is an isolated logical collection of regions (e.g., commercial vs. government realms) with separate identity — workloads cannot span realms, so government work needs a tenancy in the government realm
A realm is a billing construct — all regions in a realm share one invoice
A realm is a synonym for availability domain in older documentation
Realms are optional labels with no isolation effect
scenarios.hint: Think of realms as the highest-level isolation boundary — above even regions.
scenarios.prompt: What is a realm in OCI, and what is the practical implication?
scenarios.situation: A US federal contractor asks whether their OCI tenancy can share identity and network plumbing with their commercial workloads. They heard the phrase 'realm' and want to know if it matters.
scenarios.title: The government cloud question
scenarios.why: Realms partition OCI's global infrastructure into isolated collections of regions — the commercial realm, government realms, and others. Identity, and therefore tenancies, do not cross realm boundaries. A contractor needing government-region services must operate a tenancy inside that realm; they cannot extend a commercial tenancy into it.

choices: Put a CDN/content-delivery layer in front of the bucket (e.g., serve via edge caching) so assets are cached near users; moving the bucket helps but only for one region's users
Archive tier moves data physically closer to requestors, so switch the bucket to Archive
Object Storage is global, so the bucket location is irrelevant — the issue must be DNS
Increase the bucket's storage class to 'Performance' tier
scenarios.hint: The users are global, but the bucket is regional. What sits between them?
scenarios.prompt: What is the more targeted fix, and why?
scenarios.situation: Users in São Paulo report slow page loads for static assets served from an Object Storage bucket in us-ashburn-1. The team proposes moving the bucket to sa-saopaulo-1.
scenarios.title: The latency complaint
scenarios.why: Object Storage buckets live in a specific region; cross-ocean reads add latency. A CDN caches content at edge locations close to users worldwide, which fixes latency for all geographies at once. Moving the bucket only relocates the problem. (There is no 'Performance' tier for Object Storage — Standard and Archive are the tiers.)

choices: Resize to a smaller Flex shape (e.g., 2 OCPUs / 16 GB) — Flex shapes let you pick OCPU and memory independently instead of fixed sizes
Switch to a bare-metal shape — bare metal is always cheaper than VMs
Flex shapes are fixed at 64 OCPUs; the only fix is terminating the tenancy
Move to Dedicated VM Hosts — tenancy-level billing is cheaper
scenarios.hint: What does 'Flex' actually flex?
scenarios.prompt: What is the right compute choice, and what makes Flex shapes useful?
scenarios.situation: A team launches a VM.Standard.E5.Flex instance with 64 OCPUs and 512 GB RAM for a small internal wiki. The bill shocks them. The workload needs about 2 OCPUs.
scenarios.title: The overprovisioned VM
scenarios.why: Flex shapes (VM.Standard.E4/E5/E6.Flex) let you customize the OCPU count and memory, so you pay for what the workload needs. Fixed shapes come in preset sizes; bare metal gives a whole server (no hypervisor) for isolation/noisy-neighbor-sensitive workloads, not for saving money on a wiki.

choices: Preemptible instances — deep discount in exchange for capacity that OCI can reclaim with short notice; fine for checkpointed, resumable batch work
Reserved capacity — cheaper, but it locks the workload to a fixed shape for a year
Burstable instances — same price, better peak performance
Spot markets do not exist in OCI; the only option is on-demand
scenarios.hint: Which pricing option trades a guarantee for a discount?
scenarios.prompt: Which OCI option fits, and what is the trade-off?
scenarios.situation: A nightly ETL batch is fault-tolerant, checkpointed, and stateless — it can be interrupted and resumed. The team pays on-demand rates and wants the bill cut without code changes.
scenarios.title: The batch-job discount
scenarios.why: Preemptible instances offer steep discounts because OCI may reclaim the capacity when needed — ideal for interruptible, checkpointed batch/CI workloads. The trade-off is exactly that interruption risk. Reserved capacity is for steady-state committed use; burstable instances handle spiky CPU on small shapes, not bulk discounts.

choices: OCI Functions — serverless, event-triggered, pay-per-execution; no cluster to manage, ideal for sporadic event-driven work
OKE — cheaper because Kubernetes nodes are free
Compute VMs with cron — simplest and most 'cloud native'
Object Storage lifecycle rules can run the thumbnailing natively
scenarios.hint: Which service runs code without you provisioning anything that runs it?
scenarios.situation: Every image uploaded to an Object Storage bucket must be thumbnailed within seconds, a few hundred times a day, with zero servers to manage. The team debates OKE vs Functions.
scenarios.title: The event-driven thumbnailer
scenarios.why: OCI Functions is the serverless platform: code runs on events (like an Object Storage upload via Events service + Notifications), scales to zero, and bills per execution. OKE (managed Kubernetes) is for container orchestration you manage — overkill for a sporadic thumbnailer. Lifecycle rules manage object retention/tiering, not code execution.

choices: Instance configurations (template of launch parameters + custom image) combined with instance pools for multi-AD rollout and autoscaling
Manual launch 50 times and document the clicks in a runbook
Block volume clones — clone one volume 50 times and boot from each
IAM policies can stamp out identical instances when written per-AD
scenarios.hint: What OCI object is literally a saved 'launch this again' template?
scenarios.prompt: Which OCI features automate this repeatably?
scenarios.situation: A team must launch 50 identical web servers across 3 ADs, each from a hardened custom image with the same cloud-init bootstrap. Doing it by hand in the console is error-prone.
scenarios.title: The golden-image rollout
scenarios.why: An instance configuration captures the launch recipe (shape, image, metadata/cloud-init, networking). An instance pool uses it to launch and manage many instances across ADs/fault domains, with autoscaling and rolling updates. Custom images preserve the hardened OS state; cloud-init handles per-boot setup.

choices: OCI Bastion service — managed, time-limited SSH sessions to private instances with no public IPs or standing jump hosts; access is granted per-session and audited
Open SSH (port 22) on the database servers' public IPs with key auth
A NAT gateway — it proxies inbound SSH securely
IAM policies that allow SSH from anywhere
scenarios.hint: Which service gives you SSH to a private instance without the instance — or any jump box — having a public IP?
scenarios.situation: Engineers SSH to a public jump host, then hop to private-subnet database servers. The jump host is internet-facing with a public IP, and the security team wants that pattern gone.
scenarios.title: The SSH jump-box habit
scenarios.why: Bastion provides just-in-time SSH access to private-subnet resources without public IPs or a persistent bastion host: sessions are time-boxed, authenticated via IAM, and logged. A NAT gateway only allows outbound-initiated traffic (no inbound SSH), and public IPs on databases expand the attack surface.

choices: OS Management Hub — manages packages/errata across fleets, schedules patch jobs, and reports compliance from one place
Cloud Guard — it pushes OS patches as part of threat remediation
Block Volume backups — restoring from backup applies patches
The Events service — it emails when patches are available
scenarios.hint: Which service's whole job is 'which of my 200 servers is missing this erratum'?
scenarios.situation: 200 Oracle Linux instances across three compartments need the same security errata applied on a schedule, with a report of which instances are non-compliant. Today it's ad-hoc SSH loops.
scenarios.title: The patch Tuesday sprawl
scenarios.why: OS Management Hub is the fleet patch-management service for Oracle Linux (and Windows): register instances, define software sources, schedule patch windows, and get compliance reporting. Cloud Guard is a security-posture/threat detector, not a patcher; backups are recovery, not maintenance.

choices: Peered VCNs must have non-overlapping CIDRs — re-create one VCN with a distinct range (e.g., 10.1.0.0/16); plan IP space before peering
VCNs in different regions can never be peered
The CIDR is too large; peering requires /24 or smaller
Peering requires both VCNs to be in the same compartment
scenarios.hint: If two networks both claim 10.0.0.0/16, where does a packet to 10.0.5.7 go?
scenarios.prompt: Why, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: A company builds VCN-A (10.0.0.0/16) and VCN-B (10.0.0.0/16) in different regions, then tries to peer them so apps can talk privately. Peering creation fails.
scenarios.title: The overlapping CIDR trap
scenarios.why: VCN peering (local via LPG, or remote via DRG) routes between CIDR blocks — overlapping ranges make routes ambiguous, so OCI requires non-overlapping CIDRs (up to 5 CIDR blocks per VCN including the primary). Remote peering across regions is supported; compartment placement doesn't matter for peering, only IAM.

choices: Network Security Groups — stateful rules applied to a set of VNICs (the app tier), independent of subnet; security lists are subnet-level and stateless
A second VCN — databases must live in their own VCN
Route tables — deny routes are more precise than security rules
Change the database port — security through obscurity is sufficient
scenarios.hint: Which construct is stateful, and which one follows the VNIC instead of the subnet?
scenarios.prompt: What should they use, and what is the key difference from security lists?
scenarios.situation: A database in a private subnet accepts connections from any instance in the VCN because the security list allows 0.0.0.0/0 on port 1521. The team wants only the app tier to reach it, with rules that move with the instances.
scenarios.title: The database that answered everyone
scenarios.why: Security lists attach to subnets and are stateless (return traffic needs explicit egress rules). NSGs attach to VNICs and are stateful (return traffic is automatically allowed), and membership follows the instance, not the subnet. For tier-to-tier filtering (only app servers → DB:1521), NSGs are the precise tool.

choices: NAT gateway — allows outbound-initiated connections to the internet while blocking inbound initiation; an internet gateway requires public IPs and permits inbound
Internet gateway — private subnets can use it as long as route tables are correct
Service gateway — it proxies all internet traffic, not just OCI services
Dynamic Routing Gateway — it NATs outbound traffic automatically
scenarios.hint: Which gateway's entire purpose is 'outbound only'?
scenarios.prompt: Which gateway is correct, and why not an internet gateway?
scenarios.situation: App servers in a private subnet (no public IPs) must download OS patches from the internet, but nothing on the internet may initiate connections to them. The team considers an internet gateway.
scenarios.title: The private subnet that needed updates
scenarios.why: A NAT gateway gives private resources outbound internet access (patch downloads) with no inbound path; instances keep no public IPs. An internet gateway enables two-way traffic and needs public IPs. A service gateway reaches OCI services (Object Storage, etc.) over the private backbone — not the public internet. DRG connects to on-premises/other VCNs.

choices: Dynamic Routing Gateway — attach the VCNs and connect on-premises via Site-to-Site VPN or FastConnect; the DRG routes between them
Internet gateway on each VCN with VPN software on an instance
Local peering gateways chained VCN-to-VCN-to-datacenter
A NAT gateway with static routes to the datacenter
scenarios.hint: Which component is literally called a 'gateway' that routes between VCNs and the corporate network?
scenarios.prompt: What is the OCI hub for this, and which connection types attach to it?
scenarios.situation: A company must connect its datacenter to three OCI VCNs (prod, dev, shared-services) over a private encrypted path, with on-premises routes propagated automatically.
scenarios.title: The on-prem bridge
scenarios.why: The DRG is the regional virtual router: VCNs attach to it, and on-premises networks connect through it via IPSec Site-to-Site VPN (encrypted over internet) or FastConnect (private dedicated circuit). Remote peering between VCNs also goes through the DRG. LPGs peer VCNs but don't reach on-premises.

choices: The subnets use different DNS label configurations or the VCN's DNS label is missing — private DNS resolution of hostnames requires consistent DNS labels; check the VCN/subnet DNS settings
Instances in different subnets can never resolve each other
DNS only works with public IPs in OCI
The instances need an internet gateway for DNS
scenarios.hint: Hostname resolution in OCI depends on what label settings?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
scenarios.situation: Two instances in the same VCN can't resolve each other by hostname. DNS resolution is enabled on the VCN, and the instances are in different subnets.
scenarios.title: The hostname that wouldn't resolve
scenarios.why: OCI's private DNS resolves instance hostnames within a VCN when DNS resolution is enabled and DNS labels are set on the VCN/subnets (instances get FQDNs like host.subnet.vcn.oraclevcn.com). Missing labels or disabled resolution breaks hostname lookup; security rules don't block DNS to the VCN resolver (169.254.169.254). Cross-subnet private DNS works fine.

choices: The load-balancing policy (e.g., round-robin vs. least-connections vs. IP-hash) and session persistence settings — IP-hash or sticky sessions can pin clients to one backend
Add more backend servers — uneven traffic always means under-capacity
The VCN CIDR is too small to balance across
Health check interval — passing checks prove the policy is correct
scenarios.hint: If health checks pass but traffic is lopsided, what decides which backend gets each request?
scenarios.situation: Three web servers sit behind a load balancer, but one server gets most traffic and occasionally times out. Health checks are passing.
scenarios.title: The uneven traffic complaint
scenarios.why: OCI Load Balancer supports policies like weighted round robin, least connections, and IP hash, plus session persistence. IP-hash or sticky sessions concentrate clients on one backend even when all are healthy — that's a policy behavior, not a capacity problem. Verify the policy and persistence config before scaling.

choices: (a) Block Volumes for the database — low-latency block devices; (b) Object Storage Archive tier for backups — cheapest long-term retention, restored when needed
(a) Object Storage for the database — objects are faster than blocks; (b) Block Volumes for backups
(a) File Storage for both — NFS handles databases and backups equally
(a) Boot volumes for the database — boot volumes are optimized for data files
scenarios.hint: Databases need block devices; cold backups need the cheapest byte. Which services are which?
scenarios.prompt: Which OCI storage services fit each need?
scenarios.situation: A team needs storage for (a) a database's data files requiring low-latency block access, and (b) 10 TB of immutable nightly backups retained for years, rarely read.
scenarios.title: The backup-target debate
scenarios.why: Block Volumes provide durable, low-latency block storage for databases (attachable/detachable, with backup policies). Object Storage Archive tier is the lowest-cost option for rarely-accessed data with long retention; Standard tier is for hot data. File Storage (NFS) suits shared file workloads, not database data files.

choices: Object versioning — keeps prior versions of an object when overwritten or deleted, so the previous report is recoverable from the version history
Multipart upload — it automatically keeps a copy of each part
Pre-authenticated requests — they snapshot the bucket on each read
Replication — it copies objects to another region instantly
scenarios.hint: Which bucket setting keeps history when an object is replaced?
scenarios.prompt: What Object Storage feature would have saved them, and how does it behave?
scenarios.situation: A monthly financial report in Object Storage was overwritten by a bad upload. The team needs yesterday's version back.
scenarios.title: The overwritten report
scenarios.why: Enabling versioning on a bucket preserves earlier versions whenever an object is overwritten or deleted — you can list and restore the prior version. Replication copies data to another region for DR (doesn't help recover an overwritten object in-place), and PARs grant time-limited access, not history.

choices: A scheduled block-volume backup policy (e.g., daily incremental) assigned to the volume — automated, incremental backups with defined retention
Object Storage lifecycle rules — they back up block volumes automatically
Volume clones — clones are continuous backups
RAID inside the instance — the cloud equivalent of a backup policy
scenarios.hint: Which feature is literally a recurring schedule attached to the volume?
scenarios.prompt: What should have been in place?
scenarios.situation: A corrupted block volume took down production at 2 AM. The last manual snapshot was 3 weeks old. The DBA asks: 'Why wasn't this automatic?'
scenarios.title: The 2 AM page
scenarios.why: OCI backup policies attach to block/boot volumes and run scheduled full + incremental backups to Object Storage with retention rules — the standard automated protection. Clones are point-in-time copies (useful for dev/test), not a backup schedule. Lifecycle rules manage object retention, not volume backups.

choices: File Storage — a managed NFS file system mountable by many instances concurrently
Block Volumes — attach one volume to all 12 instances in read-write mode
Object Storage — mount it as a POSIX filesystem for config files
Boot volumes — share one boot volume across instances
scenarios.hint: Which service speaks NFS to many clients at once?
scenarios.prompt: Which OCI service replaces the rsync mesh?
scenarios.situation: Twelve web servers need read/write access to the same configuration directory and shared uploads. Each server currently rsyncs from a primary — drift and conflicts are constant.
scenarios.title: The shared-config problem
scenarios.why: File Storage provides a managed NFSv3 file system that many compute instances mount simultaneously — the native shared-filesystem answer. A block volume attaches to one instance (multi-attach is limited/specialized); Object Storage is an object API, not POSIX file semantics.

choices: Pre-authenticated request — a time-limited URL granting upload access to the bucket/prefix without an IAM identity
Make the bucket public for 30 days, then private again
Share the tenancy admin credentials with an expiry note
Object Storage lifecycle rules grant temporary write access
scenarios.hint: Which feature is a signed, expiring URL for a bucket?
scenarios.situation: An external partner must upload weekly CSVs into a private Object Storage bucket for 30 days. The team must not create an IAM user for them.
scenarios.title: The partner upload link
scenarios.why: Pre-authenticated requests (PARs) grant scoped, expiring access to a bucket or object prefix via URL — no IAM user needed. They can allow writes (uploads) as well as reads, and expire automatically. Public buckets and shared credentials are never the answer.

choices: Data Transfer service (offline disk shipment) — copy to encrypted transfer disks/devices, ship to Oracle, data is uploaded to Object Storage
Keep the 100 Mbps upload running and throttle it to business hours
Compress the archives — compression ratios guarantee it fits in a week
FastConnect — it increases the existing internet uplink speed
scenarios.hint: When the network is the bottleneck and the data is huge, what moves instead of packets?
scenarios.prompt: What is the practical OCI option?
scenarios.situation: A datacenter with a 100 Mbps uplink must move 40 TB of archives into OCI Object Storage. At current speed the transfer takes over a month, and the uplink is saturated.
scenarios.title: The 40 TB migration
scenarios.why: For bulk offline ingest, OCI's Data Transfer service ships encrypted disks (or the Transfer Appliance for petabytes) to Oracle for direct upload — far faster than a thin uplink for 40 TB. FastConnect is a private network circuit (great for steady hybrid traffic, not a magic uplink upgrade), and compression can't be assumed to fix a 37-day transfer.

choices: Design a compartment hierarchy (e.g., by environment/team) and scope policies to the least-privilege compartment — compartments are the primary isolation and policy boundary
Create more admin users so no single key is critical
Move everything to a new tenancy — compartments can't be added later
Disable IAM — it adds complexity without security benefit
scenarios.hint: What is the unit that both organizes resources and scopes policies?
scenarios.prompt: What is the foundational IAM remediation?
scenarios.situation: Everything — prod, dev, finance data — lives in the root compartment with broad admin policies. An intern's compromised key touched production.
scenarios.title: The flat-tenancy mess
scenarios.why: Compartments are OCI's fundamental organizing and isolation unit: policies grant group permissions on specific compartments, so a compromised credential scoped to dev can't reach prod. Design the hierarchy (up to 6 levels deep, including root) around blast-radius boundaries, then write least-privilege policies per compartment.

choices: Dynamic group — define the instance(s) by OCID/compartment, then write a policy granting that dynamic group access to Vault secrets and the bucket; no static credentials
Embed the API key and rotate it monthly via cron
Give the instance the tenancy admin's key — simplest
Secrets can't be read from instances; copy them at deploy time
scenarios.hint: How can an instance itself be the 'who' in a policy, with no password involved?
scenarios.prompt: What is the secure pattern, and how is it authorized?
scenarios.situation: An app on a compute instance must read secrets from Vault and write to a specific bucket. The team is tempted to bake an IAM user's API key into the image.
scenarios.title: The instance that needed a secret
scenarios.why: Dynamic groups let OCI resources (instances, functions) act as principals: matching rules select them, and policies grant the dynamic group permissions — the instance authenticates with its own identity via instance principals, no stored keys. Baking user keys into images leaks credentials to anyone with the image.

choices: Oracle secures the cloud (physical, hypervisor, network fabric); the customer secures what's IN the cloud — data, IAM policies, OS patching, security lists
Oracle handles everything above the hypervisor, including customer IAM policies
The customer handles physical datacenter security in OCI
Responsibility is split 50/50 on every control
scenarios.hint: Who configures the bucket policy — Oracle or you?
scenarios.prompt: Where does the shared responsibility line fall for IaaS?
scenarios.situation: After a misconfigured bucket leaks data, the customer tells auditors 'security is Oracle's job in the cloud.'
scenarios.title: The 'Oracle handles it' myth
scenarios.why: The shared model: Oracle owns security OF the cloud (facilities, hardware, virtualization, physical network); the customer owns security IN the cloud — their data classification, IAM least privilege, guest OS patching, firewall rules, and encryption choices. A public bucket is squarely customer-side.

choices: Cloud Guard — continuously monitors for misconfigurations and risky activity, flags problems, and can auto-remediate with responder rules
Vault — it detects misconfigurations as a side effect of key storage
Cloud Advisor — it only optimizes cost, not security
Audit logs alone — reading them daily is the intended workflow
scenarios.hint: Which service watches your tenancy and says 'that bucket shouldn't be public'?
scenarios.situation: Over months, buckets become public, ports open to 0.0.0.0/0, and keys go unrotated. The team wants continuous detection of these misconfigurations with guided remediation.
scenarios.title: The drifting configuration
scenarios.why: Cloud Guard is OCI's security-posture management: detector rules spot issues (public buckets, open security lists, etc.), and responder rules can fix them automatically. Audit service records API activity (the evidence trail); Vault stores keys/secrets. Detection + guided response is Cloud Guard's job.

choices: OCI Vault (Key Management) — create customer-managed keys, control rotation, and assign them to volumes/buckets; Oracle-managed keys are the default otherwise
Cloud Guard — it generates encryption keys during scans
IAM policies — they encrypt data at rest when written correctly
Object Storage versioning — versions are encrypted with separate keys
scenarios.hint: Which service is the key-management system, not the policy system?
scenarios.situation: Compliance requires customer-managed encryption keys for block volumes and buckets, with key rotation and no Oracle access to key material.
scenarios.title: The encryption-key question
scenarios.why: OCI encrypts data at rest by default with Oracle-managed keys. Vault (KMS) lets you create and control your own master keys — including keys backed by HSMs — and bind them to block volumes, boot volumes, and buckets, with rotation policies. IAM authorizes; it doesn't encrypt.

choices: OCI WAF for Layer-7 filtering (bot management, OWASP rules) in front of the app; OCI's edge/DDoS protection absorbs volumetric network-layer attacks
Security lists — they inspect HTTP payloads
NAT gateway — it filters inbound attack traffic
Bastion — it proxies web traffic securely
scenarios.hint: Which service understands HTTP requests, not just packets?
scenarios.prompt: Which OCI services address the network and application layers?
scenarios.situation: A public web app behind a load balancer is hit by an HTTP flood and credential-stuffing attempts. The load balancer distributes the attack evenly to all backends.
scenarios.title: The Layer-7 flood
scenarios.why: WAF inspects HTTP/S traffic against managed rules (OWASP Top 10, bots, rate limiting) before it reaches the load balancer. Network-layer DDoS absorption happens at OCI's edge. Security lists are L3/L4 packet filters (no payload inspection); NAT gateways only do outbound.

choices: Budgets with alert rules (email/notifications at thresholds) plus Cost Analysis tracking by compartment/tag — detect spend early, attribute it precisely
Delete the tenancy monthly and recreate it — guarantees zero carryover spend
Budgets hard-stop resources when exceeded — set a $0 budget
Invoices are the only cost signal OCI provides
scenarios.hint: Which two tools give you 'warn me at 80%' and 'who spent it'?
scenarios.prompt: What OCI cost-control combo prevents the next surprise?
scenarios.situation: A dev team's experiment left GPU instances running for three weeks. Finance saw it on the invoice — a month later.
scenarios.title: The surprise invoice
scenarios.why: Budgets track spend/forecast against thresholds and fire alerts (via Notifications) — they alert, they don't auto-terminate. Cost Analysis with compartment/tag grouping attributes spend to teams. Tagging resources (cost-tracking tags) is what makes the attribution work; quotas can actually cap resource counts.

choices: Quotas — set compartment-level limits on resource counts (e.g., max instances); autoscaling cannot exceed them
Budgets — they terminate instances over budget
IAM policies — they limit CPU counts directly
Cost Analysis — it rolls back excess resources
scenarios.hint: Which control says 'this compartment may never contain more than N instances'?
scenarios.prompt: What governance control caps resource creation regardless of autoscaling?
scenarios.situation: An autoscaling pool in dev has no upper bound configured in policy; a bug loops scale-out and the compartment hits the tenancy's shape limits — then the request goes to support for a limit increase, which would make it worse.
scenarios.title: The runaway autoscale
scenarios.why: Quotas enforce hard ceilings on how many of each resource type a compartment may contain — the backstop against runaway automation. Budgets only alert on spend. IAM policies authorize actions, not quantities. Combine quotas (quantity guardrail) with budgets (spend signal).

choices: Pay-as-you-go bills metered usage with no commitment; Universal Credits (monthly flex) commit to a spend level for discounted rates across eligible services — steady production fits commitment, spiky dev fits PAYG
Committed credits are only for government customers
PAYG is always cheaper regardless of usage pattern
OCI has a single pricing model; the choice is cosmetic
scenarios.hint: Which model rewards you for promising to spend?
scenarios.prompt: How do the OCI pricing models compare?
scenarios.situation: A company with steady, predictable production workloads plus spiky dev/test asks: pay-as-you-go versus committed credits?
scenarios.title: The pricing-model choice
scenarios.why: PAYG = no commitment, metered billing, maximum flexibility. Universal Credits = commit to an amount (monthly flex or annual) for lower rates, usable across many services — the discount rewards predictable spend. Match steady-state production to commitment and variable dev/test to PAYG.

choices: Always Free includes limited compute (Ampere/micro VMs), Autonomous Database instances, storage, and more — but verify current limits/regions; exceeding them bills at PAYG rates
Always Free covers unlimited usage of every service for students
Always Free requires a paid support plan
Free tier resources can't run databases
scenarios.hint: Free within limits — what happens past the limits?
scenarios.prompt: What does Always Free offer, and what is the catch to verify?
scenarios.situation: A student wants to prototype on OCI for a semester project with zero budget: a small VM, an Oracle database, and some object storage.
scenarios.title: The free-tier prototype
scenarios.why: OCI Always Free provides a set of resources (compute VMs, Autonomous Databases, block/object storage, load balancer, etc.) free for the tenancy's life within published limits. The discipline: know the limits (e.g., VM counts/shapes, storage GB) because overages bill at PAYG — and check the current published terms, which Oracle can change.

choices: Defined (tag-namespace) cost-tracking tags applied at creation, enforced by policy/IAM, grouped in Cost Analysis — freeform tags work but defined tags are governable
Rename all resources with project prefixes — names are the cost signal
Compartments alone are enough; tags add nothing
Budgets automatically infer project ownership
scenarios.hint: Which metadata, applied to resources, does Cost Analysis group by?
scenarios.situation: Finance sees a 40% cost jump but can't tell which project caused it — resources have no consistent labels, and several teams share compartments.
scenarios.title: The mystery spend
scenarios.why: Cost-tracking tags let Cost Analysis slice spend by project/team/owner. Defined tags (under a tag namespace) can be restricted by IAM so only finance's namespace values are used — preventing tag sprawl. Require tags at creation (via policy or process) or attribution stays guesswork.

choices: Higher support tiers offer faster response SLAs and more channels — but choose the tier before the incident; know your current SLA and escalation path now
All tiers have identical 15-minute response for any severity
Support tiers only differ in documentation access
Upgrading mid-incident retroactively speeds up the current ticket
scenarios.hint: When is the right time to learn your support SLA — during the outage or before?
scenarios.prompt: What should they know about OCI support tiers?
scenarios.situation: Production is down at 3 AM. The team has basic OCI support and wonders whether they can get a faster response by 'upgrading mid-incident'.
scenarios.title: The 3 AM severity-1
scenarios.why: OCI support comes in tiers with different response-time targets, channels, and features (e.g., basic vs. paid tiers with faster Sev-1 response). The operational lesson: know your tier's SLA and escalation procedure before you need it; you can't negotiate response times during an outage.

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Oracle Oci as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Regions & ADs Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Regions & ADs is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Regions & ADs?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Regions & ADs issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Regions & ADs is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Regions & ADs supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Regions & ADs failure in Oracle Oci.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Regions & ADs
evidence: All Regions & ADs components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

domains.name: Start Here
domains.description: How to use this bootcamp, study strategy for the OCI Architect Associate exam, and the OCI lab environment guide.

scenarios.title: Navigating the bootcamp
scenarios.situation: You're new to OCI and want the Architect Associate certification in 8 weeks, studying 6 hours a week.
scenarios.prompt: What's the right first two weeks?
choices: Jump to containers-OKE — it's the most modern topic
Take mock assessments first to benchmark
Read all lessons across 15 domains before touching labs
Start-here (all 4 lessons), then IAM/security and networking in order — IAM policies gate everything and VCN design underlies compute/storage; build the service-chooser note from day one
scenarios.why: Dependency order dominates OCI learning: IAM and networking are prerequisites for nearly every scenario question. The blueprint weights them heavily too, so front-loading them is both pedagogically and strategically correct.
scenarios.hint: Which domains do all the others assume?

scenarios.title: Planning study time
scenarios.situation: You have 6 hours a week. You want to pass, not just learn.
choices: All scenarios, no lessons
Cram everything in the last two weeks
2h lessons, 2h labs, 2h scenarios — the exam tests design judgment under options, and scenarios train exactly that; labs build the console intuition that makes service questions fast
6h of lessons; labs later
scenarios.why: The exam is scenario-heavy: 'which service/design' questions reward practiced judgment. An even three-way split builds knowledge (lessons), intuition (labs), and judgment (scenarios) together.
scenarios.hint: What question shape dominates the exam?
evidence: Lessons + labs + scenarios in balance; judgment is trained

scenarios.title: Using labs effectively
scenarios.situation: A lab asks you to create a VCN, but you've only read about VCNs.
choices: Skip the lab — scenarios matter more
Copy a friend's lab output
Do the lab now — use the console's Copy-as-CLI to learn the commands, tag everything, then break it and rebuild once; the rebuild is where the mental model forms
Re-read the networking lessons until confident
scenarios.why: Labs convert declarative knowledge into mental models, and rebuilding after breaking cements them. The console-to-CLI path teaches real syntax; tagging builds the cost habit the exam tests.
scenarios.hint: When does the mental model actually form?

scenarios.title: Mock exam strategy
scenarios.situation: First mock: 68%. The exam needs ~65-70% depending on the form. Three weeks left.
choices: Take a mock every day until it clicks
Memorize the mock questions
Focus on your strongest domains
Analyze misses by domain — drill the two weakest domains fully (lessons + labs + scenarios), update the service-chooser note with each miss's rule, then re-mock; targeted loops beat blanket review
scenarios.why: Miss analysis by domain turns a score into a study plan. Each miss becomes a service-chooser rule, so the note compounds. Daily mocks without review just rehearse the same gaps.
scenarios.hint: What does a miss become in your system?
evidence: Miss -> domain drill -> service-chooser rule -> re-mock

domains.name: Mock Assessment
domains.description: Timed assessment shell — scenarios are drawn from all domains at runtime.

domains.name: Capstone: 3-Tier App on OCI
domains.description: Design and deploy a production-style 3-tier application on OCI: network, compute, database, security, and cost controls.

scenarios.title: Capstone: network design decision
scenarios.situation: Phase 1: your web tier needs internet access, app and DB tiers must not be directly reachable. You have one VCN.
choices: Private subnets for all tiers including web, with a VPN for users
Public subnet (web) with internet gateway; private subnets (app, DB) with NAT gateway for outbound-only; security lists/NSGs enforcing web->app->DB flow with default deny elsewhere
All tiers in one public subnet, secured by passwords
Three VCNs, one per tier, peered together
scenarios.why: The public/private subnet split with IGW/NAT is the canonical 3-tier pattern: web reachable inbound, app/DB outbound-only for patches. NSGs enforce the tier-to-tier matrix. Three VCNs add peering complexity for no benefit.
scenarios.hint: Which gateway gives private subnets outbound-only access?
evidence: Public web + private app/DB, IGW + NAT, NSG matrix

scenarios.title: Capstone: database choice
scenarios.situation: The app needs a relational database, ~50GB, variable load, no DBA on the team.
choices: DB System VM — cheapest always
MySQL HeatWave — it's MySQL
Block volume with manual MySQL install
Autonomous Database Serverless — auto-scaling, auto-patching, no admin overhead; fits variable load and the no-DBA constraint; DB Systems would need patching labor, HeatWave is the wrong workload
scenarios.why: Service choice follows constraints: variable load wants elasticity, no-DBA wants autonomy — Autonomous Serverless matches both. The exam rewards matching service properties to stated constraints, not brand preference.
scenarios.hint: Which constraints point to Autonomous?
evidence: Variable load + no DBA = Autonomous Serverless

scenarios.title: Capstone: scaling the web tier
scenarios.situation: Launch went well; traffic spikes 10x for 2 hours daily. The web tier is a fixed 4 instances.
choices: Instance pool with autoscaling policy (CPU-based) behind the load balancer — capacity tracks demand; fixed instances either waste money or drop traffic, and manual resizing doesn't react in minutes
Bigger fixed instances
Over-provision 40 instances permanently
Ask users to come back later
scenarios.why: Autoscaling matches capacity to the demand curve — the cost-effective answer to spiky traffic. Fixed capacity can't do both cheap and reliable; the pool + LB + policy is the exam's canonical scaling pattern.
scenarios.hint: What metric commonly drives the scaling policy?
evidence: Instance pool + autoscaling + LB for spiky web traffic

scenarios.title: Capstone: cost overrun
scenarios.situation: Month 1 bill is 3x the budget. Untagged resources everywhere, one always-on GPU instance 'for testing'.
choices: Just raise the budget
Terminate the database
Tag everything and analyze cost by tag to find the drivers; terminate/right-size the GPU instance; set budget alerts; then right-size the pool minimums — measure first, cut second, alert always
Delete everything and start over
scenarios.why: Cost discipline is measure-then-cut: tagging reveals the drivers (the GPU instance), rightsizing follows, and budget alerts prevent recurrence. Raising the budget without analysis just funds the waste.
scenarios.hint: What must come before cutting costs?

scenarios.title: Capstone: security review
scenarios.situation: Before demo day: DB port open to 0.0.0.0/0 'temporarily', credentials in instance metadata, one public object bucket.
choices: Demo first, fix later
Fail the review — all three are blockers: restrict DB ingress to the app NSG, move credentials to Vault, make the bucket private; re-verify each with the documented check before sign-off
Pass with notes — it's just a capstone
Fix the bucket; the rest is fine
scenarios.why: Security checklists are binary: each item passes or blocks. 'Temporary' open database ports and credentials in metadata are exactly how real breaches start — the capstone practices production standards, not demo standards.
scenarios.hint: Why are checklist items binary?
evidence: Blockers block — verify each fix before sign-off

domains.name: Database Services
domains.description: Autonomous Database, DB Systems, MySQL HeatWave, and data management on OCI.

scenarios.title: Choosing the database service
scenarios.situation: New SaaS app: relational data, 200GB, spiky traffic (10x daily peaks), team of 5 with no DBA.
choices: Autonomous Database Serverless (ATP) — auto-scales with the spikes, self-patching covers the no-DBA constraint, relational fits; DB Systems would need DBA labor, HeatWave is analytics
DB System bare metal — maximum control
MySQL HeatWave — cheapest headline price
Self-managed MySQL on a compute instance
scenarios.why: Constraints decide: spiky = elastic scaling, no DBA = autonomous operations, relational = ATP. Each rejected option fails a stated constraint — that's the exam's selection logic.
scenarios.hint: Which constraints eliminate DB Systems?
evidence: Spiky + no DBA + relational = Autonomous Serverless

scenarios.title: Zero data loss requirement
scenarios.situation: Core banking ledger: RPO must be zero, RTO under 5 minutes, cross-region.
choices: Autonomous Data Guard across regions (or manual Data Guard with fast-start failover) — synchronous replication gives zero data loss; cross-region covers region failure; RAC alone doesn't cross regions
Nightly backups to object storage
RAC within one AD
Async replication with 1-hour lag
scenarios.why: RPO zero requires synchronous replication — Data Guard in max-availability mode. Cross-region needs the standby in another region. Backups and async replication both admit data loss; RAC doesn't span regions.
scenarios.hint: What replication mode gives RPO zero?
evidence: RPO 0 = synchronous Data Guard; cross-region = remote standby

scenarios.title: Oops recovery
scenarios.situation: A bad deployment corrupted order data at 2 PM; discovered at 4 PM. The database is Autonomous.
choices: Point-in-time recovery to 1:55 PM (before the corruption) — Autonomous PITR to any 5-minute window in retention; verify the recovered data, then replay legitimate 2-4 PM transactions from app logs
Restore last night's backup — lose a full day
Manually fix the corrupted rows
Fail over to Data Guard standby (has the same corruption)
scenarios.why: PITR targets just-before-corruption — minimal data loss, no full rebuild. The standby replicated the corruption (it's a replica, not a time machine); manual fixes don't scale to unknown corruption extent.
scenarios.hint: Why doesn't the standby help here?
evidence: Logical corruption -> PITR, not standby (replica has it too)

scenarios.title: Dev data refresh
scenarios.situation: Developers need production-like data; compliance forbids real customer data in dev.
choices: Point dev at production (read-only)
Clone the Autonomous DB (thin clone, minutes), mask/anonymize sensitive columns in the clone, hand the masked clone to dev — production-like shape, compliant content, fast provisioning
Copy the production DB as-is to dev
Hand-craft fake data (months of work)
scenarios.why: Clone + mask is the standard: thin clones are fast and storage-cheap, masking satisfies compliance, and developers get realistic data volumes and distributions. Each alternative fails speed, compliance, or safety.
scenarios.hint: What makes thin clones ideal for dev refresh?
evidence: Thin clone -> mask -> dev; fast, cheap, compliant

scenarios.title: Insecure database exposure
scenarios.situation: Review finds the production ATP with a public endpoint, wallet shared in the team chat.
choices: Move the database to another compartment
Private endpoint in the VCN (remove public access), per-service wallets with rotation (revoke the shared one), NSG allowing 1521 only from app tier — network, credential, and access layers all fixed
Change the admin password
It's fine — the wallet is password-protected
scenarios.why: Three independent failures need three fixes: public endpoint (network), shared wallet (credential hygiene), and the NSG rule (access scope). Password rotation alone leaves the network exposure; compartment moves change nothing.
scenarios.hint: Which three layers failed here?
evidence: Private endpoint + wallet rotation + NSG scoping

scenarios.title: Patching burden
scenarios.situation: Team spends 2 days monthly patching DB Systems; a patching mistake caused last quarter's outage.
choices: Patch faster — skip staging
Hire a DBA for patching
Stop patching — stability over security

Migrate suitable workloads to Autonomous (self-patching) — eliminates the patching labor and the human-error outage class; keep DB Systems only where version/control needs demand it, with staged patching
scenarios.why: Autonomous removes the entire patching burden class — labor and outage risk together. The decision framework: which workloads actually need DB Systems' control? The rest migrate; the remainder get staged, scheduled patching.
scenarios.hint: What two costs does Autonomous eliminate here?
evidence: Autonomous for the patchable; staged process for the rest

scenarios.title: Analytics on MySQL
scenarios.situation: MySQL app now needs real-time dashboards over the transactional data; nightly ETL to a warehouse is too slow.
choices: Enable HeatWave on the MySQL DB System — in-memory analytics accelerator on the same MySQL, no ETL, real-time OLAP on OLTP data; separate warehouse keeps the latency problem
Bigger MySQL instance
Export to CSV hourly for the dashboards
Migrate to ADW (rewrite the app)
scenarios.why: HeatWave's value proposition is exactly this: analytics acceleration inside MySQL, eliminating the ETL pipeline. Bigger instances don't add OLAP capability; rewrites are disproportionate.
scenarios.hint: What does HeatWave eliminate?
evidence: Real-time MySQL analytics without ETL = HeatWave

domains.name: Containers and OKE
domains.description: Container Instances, Oracle Container Engine for Kubernetes, and container registry.

scenarios.title: OKE or Container Instances?
scenarios.situation: Nightly ETL job: one container, runs 2 hours, then idle 22 hours.
choices: Container Instances — single container, batch schedule, idle 22h (per-second billing, zero idle cost); an OKE cluster for one nightly job is operational overkill
OKE cluster with one node
Always-on compute instance
Bare metal server
scenarios.why: Complexity follows need: one batch container needs no orchestration, no nodes, no cluster patching. Per-second billing matches the 2h/day profile; always-on options bill 24h for 2h of work.
scenarios.hint: What workload shape fits Container Instances?
evidence: Single container + batch + idle = Container Instances

scenarios.title: Node pool design
scenarios.situation: Cluster runs web pods (steady), ML training (GPU, bursty), and batch (nightly spikes).
choices: Three pools: general (web, autoscaled), GPU pool (ML, scaled to zero when idle), virtual nodes or autoscaled pool for batch — workload-shaped pools with independent scaling; one pool forces one shape on all
One big pool of GPU instances for everything
Manual node management per workload
Virtual nodes for the steady web tier
scenarios.why: Heterogeneous workloads need heterogeneous pools — GPU for ML only (cost), autoscaling for steady web, scale-to-zero/burst for batch. One pool means paying GPU prices for web pods or CPU limits for training.
scenarios.hint: Why not one pool for everything?
evidence: Pool per workload shape; scale each independently

scenarios.title: Insecure image pipeline
scenarios.situation: Prod deploys pull :latest from a public repo, no scanning, no signing.
choices: Private OCIR repos, vulnerability scanning on push (block criticals), immutable version tags (no :latest in prod), image signing with in-cluster verification — supply chain from storage to admission
Just switch to :stable tag
Scanning is enough
Sign images but keep public pulls
scenarios.why: Supply-chain security is layered: private storage, scan gates, immutable tags (rollback needs them), and signature admission. Each layer covers a different attack (tampering, CVEs, tag mutation).
scenarios.hint: Why is :latest dangerous in production?

scenarios.title: CrashLooping pods
scenarios.situation: Web pods CrashLoop after a deploy; the deploy changed only an env var.
choices: Restart the cluster
Scale up the nodes
Roll back without investigating

kubectl get events (schedule/failure reasons), kubectl logs --previous (crash output), describe the pod (probe failures, bad env) — events + logs + describe is the triage trio; the env var is the prime suspect
scenarios.why: Container triage is events -> logs -> describe: the scheduler and kubelet explain most crashes. The changed env var focuses the search — verify with logs before rolling back blindly.
scenarios.hint: What three commands form the triage trio?

scenarios.title: Pod-to-pod breach
scenarios.situation: A compromised frontend pod reached the database pod directly; no network policies exist.
choices: Default-deny network policies per namespace with explicit allows (frontend->API, API->DB only) — microsegmentation for pods, mirroring the NSG tier matrix one level down
Bigger cluster
Move the database out of the cluster
Firewall the nodes
scenarios.why: Flat pod networking is the default — network policies are the segmentation control. Default-deny with explicit allows replicates the tier matrix inside the cluster; node firewalls don't see pod-to-pod traffic properly.
scenarios.hint: What's the pod equivalent of NSGs?

scenarios.title: Secrets in YAML
scenarios.situation: Deployments mount DB passwords as plain env vars in committed YAML.
choices: Private git repo (still in git)
Env vars are fine — YAML is internal
OCI Vault for the secrets, injected via the secrets-store CSI driver (or sealed secrets) — secrets never in git, never in plain YAML; etcd encryption at rest as the backstop
Base64-encode them (still plain)
scenarios.why: Base64 is encoding, not encryption; private repos still leak. Vault-backed injection keeps secrets out of manifests and git entirely — the only answer that survives a repo leak.
scenarios.hint: Why doesn't base64 count as protection?

scenarios.title: Slow scaling response
scenarios.situation: Traffic spike: HPA adds pods in 1 min, but new nodes take 8 min — requests queue.
choices: Faster node shapes
Disable HPA
Pre-warm the maximum nodes always
Over-provision headroom (buffer nodes) + virtual nodes for burst (per-pod, no node wait) — node provisioning latency is structural; buffers and serverless pods absorb the spike while nodes catch up
scenarios.why: Two scaling speeds exist: pods (fast) and nodes (slow). Virtual nodes eliminate the node wait for burst; buffer headroom covers the gap. Always-max nodes waste the steady-state budget.
scenarios.hint: Which scales faster — pods or nodes?
evidence: Pods fast, nodes slow — buffer + virtual nodes for burst

domains.name: Observability and Monitoring
domains.description: Monitoring, alarms, logging, events, and health checks across OCI resources.

scenarios.title: Alarm design
scenarios.situation: Web tier: need to know about outages before users report them, without 3 AM false pages.
choices: No alarms — dashboards suffice
LB healthy-backend count + 5xx rate + p99 latency, with sensible thresholds and notification topics per severity — user-impact signals, not raw CPU; paging only on user-facing symptoms
CPU > 50% pages the on-call
Disk > 90% emails everyone
scenarios.why: Alarm on user impact (errors, latency, healthy backends), not infrastructure trivia — CPU spikes don't page, 5xx spikes do. Severity-routed notifications keep pages meaningful.
scenarios.hint: What should page vs what should email?
evidence: Page on user impact; email on early warnings

scenarios.title: Log strategy
scenarios.situation: Microservices on OKE: developers SSH into pods to read logs.
choices: Stdout/stderr collection to OCI Logging from day one — centralized, searchable, retained; pod-local logs die with the pod and SSH-to-pod doesn't scale past three services
Bigger pod disks for log files
Log to files on a shared volume
Email logs on error
scenarios.why: Centralized logging is structural: pods are ephemeral, so pod-local logs are unreliable by design. Stdout collection + central search is the pattern; everything else fights the platform.
scenarios.hint: Why are pod-local logs unreliable?
evidence: Stdout -> central Logging; pods are ephemeral

scenarios.title: Slow requests
scenarios.situation: p99 latency doubled; metrics show all services 'healthy', logs show nothing obvious.
choices: More metrics dashboards
Restart all services
Add more instances
Distributed tracing — follow a slow request across service hops; metrics aggregate away the slow hop, logs show single-service views; the trace reveals which hop regressed
scenarios.why: Latency across services needs request-scoped visibility — traces show per-hop timing that aggregated metrics hide. 'All healthy' metrics with slow requests is the classic trace-shaped problem.
scenarios.hint: What do traces show that metrics hide?
evidence: Per-hop timing for slow requests = tracing

scenarios.title: Automated response
scenarios.situation: Requirement: when a compute instance is deleted, snapshot its boot volume first.
choices: A cron job checking hourly
Manual runbook
Disable instance deletion
Events service rule matching instance-delete, triggering a Functions function that creates the snapshot — event-driven automation; the rule watches, the function acts
scenarios.why: Events + Functions is OCI's automation pair: the event fires in real time, the function executes the response. Cron polls (with gaps); manual runbooks don't scale; disabling deletion breaks legitimate workflows.
scenarios.hint: Which two services form the automation pair?

scenarios.title: Health check design
scenarios.situation: LB health checks hit / and get 200 from the web server — but the app behind it is down.
choices: More frequent shallow checks
Bigger health-check timeout
Remove health checks
Deep health endpoint (/health) that checks app + DB connectivity — the LB should route on application health, not web-server liveness; shallow checks hide outages
scenarios.why: Health checks must reflect the dependency chain: web-up/app-down is exactly the failure shallow checks miss. The endpoint should fail when the app can't serve — that's the signal the LB needs.
scenarios.hint: What should /health verify?
evidence: Check the full serving path, not just the web server

scenarios.title: Dashboard for executives
scenarios.situation: Leadership wants a service health view; engineers have 40 detailed dashboards.
choices: Share all 40 dashboards
No dashboard — weekly email
Executive view of raw metrics
One executive dashboard: user-facing SLOs (availability, p99, error budget), traffic, and incident status — business signals, not pod CPU; link to engineering dashboards for drill-down
scenarios.why: Audience determines content: executives need SLOs and business impact, engineers need the 40. One curated view with drill-down links serves both without drowning either.
scenarios.hint: What belongs on an executive dashboard?
evidence: SLOs + business signals up top; drill-down below

scenarios.title: Observability cost

choices: One year retention for everything 'just in case'
Stop logging

Log levels per environment (info+ in prod, debug only when troubleshooting), retention tiers (hot 30d, archive after), and sampling for high-volume low-value logs — verbosity and retention are the cost levers
Delete all logs
scenarios.why: Observability has a cost curve: level, volume, and retention multiply. Production needs info-level with short hot retention; debug is a troubleshooting mode, not a default. The levers are explicit and adjustable.
scenarios.hint: What three levers control logging cost?
evidence: Level x volume x retention — tune all three

domains.name: Backup and Disaster Recovery
domains.description: Backups, cross-region copy, replication, and DR architectures on OCI.

scenarios.title: Numbers first
scenarios.situation: A team debates backup tools for the order database. One engineer wants hourly snapshots; another wants Data Guard; a third says nightly backups are fine.
choices: Whatever the team knows best
The most advanced technology
The business's RPO/RTO: 'lose at most 5 minutes, down at most 30' rules out nightly backups and selects Data Guard or frequent snapshots — the numbers choose the method
The cheapest option
scenarios.why: RPO/RTO are the selection criteria — without them the debate is preferences. 5-minute RPO needs near-continuous replication; the numbers eliminate options mechanically.
scenarios.hint: Who sets RPO/RTO — engineering or the business?
evidence: RPO/RTO first; the numbers select the method

scenarios.title: RTO 20 minutes
scenarios.situation: Checkout database: RPO 5 min, RTO 20 min, single region acceptable.
choices: Warm standby (scaled-down live copy, Data Guard sync for 5-min RPO) scaled up on failover — 20-min RTO needs live infra, not deploy-from-scratch; pilot light's deploy time risks the RTO
Nightly backup restore
Pilot light with IaC deploy
Active-active dual write
scenarios.why: 20-minute RTO rules out deploy-from-scratch (pilot light) and restore-from-backup; warm standby's live-but-small footprint fails over in minutes. 5-min RPO needs sync/near-sync replication.
scenarios.hint: What RTO threshold separates pilot light from warm standby?
evidence: RTO < ~30min -> warm standby; hours -> pilot light

scenarios.title: Ransomware-proof backups
scenarios.situation: After a near-miss ransomware incident, leadership asks: 'are our backups safe?'
choices: Antivirus on the backup server
Immutable retention rules on backup buckets + separate-compartment storage with delete-restricted IAM + cross-region copies — demonstrated by the config, not asserted; plus a restore drill report
'We have backups'
More frequent backups (still deletable)
scenarios.why: Backup safety is proven by controls: immutability (can't be encrypted), separation (different blast radius), and tested restores (they actually work). Frequency without immutability just makes more deletable copies.
scenarios.hint: Why doesn't frequency alone help?
evidence: Immutable + separated + tested — frequency is secondary

scenarios.title: The failed drill
scenarios.situation: DR drill: planned RTO 30 min, actual 90 min. Gaps: DNS TTL 1 hour, runbook missing the LB step, one stale credential.
choices: Accept 90 min as the real RTO
Blame the team
Skip the next drill — too disruptive
Fix all three (TTL to 60s, runbook update, credential rotation process), re-drill in 90 days — the drill's value is the gap list; unaddressed gaps make the next drill fail identically
scenarios.why: Drills exist to produce gap lists — each gap has a concrete fix, and the re-drill verifies. Accepting 90 minutes rewrites the objective without business approval; skipping drills guarantees the next real failover finds the same gaps.
scenarios.hint: What is a drill's actual deliverable?

scenarios.title: Tiering the workloads
scenarios.situation: CFO: 'DR for everything at Tier-1 level costs $2M/year. Cut it.'
choices: Tier the workloads: Tier 1 (orders DB, 5-min RPO) keeps premium DR; Tier 2 (analytics, 24h RPO) gets backup-restore; Tier 3 (dev) gets best-effort — present the tiered cost vs the uniform cost with risk per tier
Cut DR for everything equally
Keep uniform Tier-1 — safety first
Drop DR entirely
scenarios.why: Tiering aligns DR spend with business impact — the CFO's cut becomes a risk-tiering conversation, not a binary. Uniform premium DR wastes most of the $2M on workloads that don't need it.
scenarios.hint: How do you turn a cost cut into a risk decision?
evidence: Tier by impact; price each tier; let risk decide

scenarios.title: PITR vs backup
scenarios.situation: A developer dropped the wrong table at 10 AM; the nightly backup ran at 2 AM.
choices: Restore the 2 AM backup — accept 8h loss
Recreate the table from memory
Replay the day's transactions manually
Point-in-time recovery to 9:55 AM — loses 5 minutes, not 8 hours; the nightly backup is the fallback if PITR's window doesn't cover it
scenarios.why: PITR minimizes loss to minutes when the window covers the incident — it's the precision tool. Full backup restore is the blunt fallback. The choice is mechanical: finest-grained recovery that covers the point.
scenarios.hint: When is full restore better than PITR?
evidence: Finest granularity that covers the incident point

scenarios.title: Schrödinger's backup
scenarios.situation: Backups have run nightly for a year. Nobody has ever restored one.
choices: Needs more frequent backups
Needs longer retention
Unverified — schedule a restore test immediately; until a restore succeeds, the program's status is unknown, and the exam treats untested backups as no backups
Healthy — a year of green checkmarks
scenarios.why: Backup success and restore success are different things — only restores prove recoverability. A year of untested backups is a year of assumptions; the restore test converts assumption to evidence.
scenarios.hint: What proves a backup program works?
evidence: Untested backup = unknown backup; restore tests prove it

scenarios.title: Reading the stem
scenarios.situation: Stem: 'A company needs a highly available web application with minimal operational overhead. Traffic is spiky.'
scenarios.prompt: Which constraints matter and what do they select?
choices: HA + minimal ops + spiky -> multi-AD instance pool with autoscaling behind a load balancer, managed services throughout — each qualifier eliminates options (fixed instances fail spiky; self-managed fails minimal-ops)
HA alone matters — biggest instances in one AD
Minimal ops means serverless everything regardless
Spiky means over-provision for the peak
scenarios.why: Multi-qualifier stems need all qualifiers satisfied: HA kills single-AD, minimal-ops kills self-managed, spiky kills fixed capacity. The correct option is the intersection, found by elimination.
scenarios.hint: How do you use multiple qualifiers?
evidence: Each qualifier eliminates options; take the intersection

scenarios.title: Elimination drill
scenarios.situation: Four options for a database question; you recognize two as violating stated constraints.
choices: Pick the first remaining option
Guess randomly between all four
Eliminate the two violators, then compare the remaining two against the subtler constraints (cost, ops overhead) — elimination first narrows the field, then precision decides
Pick the longest option
scenarios.why: Elimination converts 4-option questions into 2-option questions — your odds double before you even decide. The remaining comparison uses the secondary qualifiers the stem provided.
scenarios.hint: What does elimination do to your odds?
evidence: Kill constraint-violators first; decide among survivors

scenarios.title: Select THREE
scenarios.situation: Question says 'Select THREE'. You've confidently identified two correct options; the remaining three are uncertain.
choices: Pick the two and move on
Select all five to be safe
Guess the third randomly without re-reading
Re-read the stem for the third constraint you missed — 'select N' questions have N constraints; the uncertain options map to the constraint you haven't applied yet
scenarios.why: 'Select N' means N independent reasons — the stem contains them all. The missing pick corresponds to the unread constraint; re-reading with 'what's the third requirement' finds it.
scenarios.hint: What does the count tell you about the stem?
evidence: N picks = N constraints; find each in the stem

scenarios.title: The public database
scenarios.situation: An architecture diagram shows the database in a public subnet with 0.0.0.0/0 ingress. The question asks what's wrong.
choices: Note it as minor
The diagram is probably simplified

Flag it as the primary issue — public database with open ingress violates every security baseline; the fix (private subnet, NSG from app tier only) is the expected answer regardless of what else the question asks
It's fine for the exam

scenarios.hint: What makes this 'always wrong'?
evidence: Public DB + open ingress = automatic finding

scenarios.title: The 40-line config
scenarios.situation: Question 12 presents a 40-line IAM policy and asks what it allows. You've spent 2 minutes.
choices: Flag and move on — 2 minutes is over budget; return with remaining time when the easy marks are banked; the policy parses the same in minute 80 as in minute 12
Keep parsing — you're almost there
Guess without reading
Skip the exam's policy questions entirely
scenarios.why: Time discipline is per-question: the budget is ~90 seconds, and sunk time doesn't earn marks. Flagged questions get fresh eyes later; the opportunity cost of one monster question is three easy ones.
scenarios.hint: What's the per-question budget?
evidence: Flag, guess, move on — budget protects the other 40

scenarios.title: Pattern recognition
scenarios.situation: Stem: 'Design a highly available web tier: traffic across two ADs, automatic recovery from instance failure, health-based routing.'
choices: Instance pool across ADs with autoscaling, public load balancer with health checks on /health — the canonical HA web tier
One large instance in each AD with DNS round-robin
Two instances behind a NAT gateway
A single instance with a backup taken hourly
scenarios.why: Pool + LB + health checks is the textbook HA web tier: instances span ADs, failures are detected and replaced, traffic routes only to healthy backends. DNS round-robin has no health awareness; NAT gateways don't balance; single instances aren't HA.
scenarios.hint: Which components provide health-aware routing?
evidence: HA web = pool + autoscaling + LB + health checks

scenarios.title: Cost with guardrails
scenarios.situation: Stem: 'Reduce compute spend 30% for dev/test environments. Production is untouched. Which combination works?'
choices: Burstable shapes with stop schedules for nights/weekends — dev/test tolerates both, production isolation keeps the guardrail
Move production to preemptible instances
Delete all backups to save storage spend
Reduce the production pool's minimum instance count
scenarios.why: Dev/test tolerates burstable throttling and stopped nights — the 30% comes from matching spend to tolerance, with production explicitly untouched. The other options all raid production availability or recoverability, violating the guardrail.

lessons.title: Regions & ADs — Core concepts
concepts: Availability domains: the pattern: replicate across ADs for site resilience, and across fault domains inside an AD for hardware resilience. Fault domains are intra-AD resilience (independent racks, shared datacenter infrastructure), while regions are independent geographies.

Fault domains: within an AD, three fault domains group racks on different hardware, so a rack failure affects only one fault domain. Surviving a region-level event requires a second region (e.g., async replication to a paired region), not more fault domains.

Regions: realms partition OCI's global infrastructure into isolated collections of regions — the commercial realm, government realms, and others. You can subscribe to other regions for compute, storage, and networking workloads, but IAM (users, groups, compartments, policies) is anchored to the home region.
Disaster recovery scope: match the failure scope to the isolation construct.
OCI's distributed cloud includes Dedicated Region (a complete OCI region in the customer's datacenter), Oracle Alloy (partners run their own cloud), and Roving Edge for disconnected edge sites.

Dedicated Region is the answer for strict residency plus cloud services on-premises; a public region in the same country may satisfy residency but not the behind-the-firewall requirement. The home region is chosen at signup and is immutable: it hosts the tenancy's IAM definitions.

lessons.title: Storage — Core concepts
concepts: Block Volumes provide durable, low-latency block storage for databases (attachable/detachable, with backup policies). OCI backup policies attach to block/boot volumes and run scheduled full + incremental backups to Object Storage with retention rules — the standard automated protection.

Object Storage tiers: a block volume attaches to one instance (multi-attach is limited/specialized); Object Storage is an object API, not POSIX file semantics. Object Storage Archive tier is the lowest-cost option for rarely-accessed data with long retention; Standard tier is for hot data.

Object versioning: enabling versioning on a bucket preserves earlier versions whenever an object is overwritten or deleted — you can list and restore the prior version. Pre-authenticated requests (PARs) grant scoped, expiring access to a bucket or object prefix via URL — no IAM user needed.

Data protection: file Storage (NFS) suits shared file workloads, not database data files. For bulk offline ingest, OCI's Data Transfer service ships encrypted disks (or the Transfer Appliance for petabytes) to Oracle for direct upload — far faster than a thin uplink for 40 TB.
Backup policies: clones are point-in-time copies (useful for dev/test), not a backup schedule.
Block volume backups: lifecycle rules manage object retention, not volume backups.

lessons.title: IAM & Security — Core concepts
concepts: Compartments are OCI's fundamental organizing and isolation unit: policies grant group permissions on specific compartments, so a compromised credential scoped to dev can't reach prod.

Least privilege: the shared model: Oracle owns security OF the cloud (facilities, hardware, virtualization, physical network); the customer owns security IN the cloud — their data classification, IAM least privilege, guest OS patching, firewall rules, and encryption choices.

Dynamic groups let OCI resources (instances, functions) act as principals: matching rules select them, and policies grant the dynamic group permissions — the instance authenticates with its own identity via instance principals, no stored keys.

Shared security model: cloud Guard is OCI's security-posture management: detector rules spot issues (public buckets, open security lists, etc.), and responder rules can fix them automatically. Security lists are L3/L4 packet filters (no payload inspection); NAT gateways only do outbound.
Cloud Guard: detection + guided response is Cloud Guard's job.

lessons.title: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure - Core concepts
concepts: A tenancy is the root of your OCI footprint; compartments are the isolation units inside it. Put environments and teams in their own compartments so IAM policies express least privilege and cost tracking stays clean.

IAM is users in groups, granted by policies written as 'Allow group X to <verb> <resource> in compartment Y'. Verbs ascend inspect < use < manage; dynamic groups let instances call OCI APIs without storing credentials.

A VCN is your private network: a CIDR block carved into subnets, with route tables and gateways. Public subnets route through an internet gateway; private subnets use a NAT gateway for outbound-only traffic or a service gateway for Oracle services.

Security lists apply at the subnet level and need explicit return rules; network security groups attach to individual VNICs for finer control. Layer them: broad subnet rules outside, precise NSG rules inside.

OKE is managed Kubernetes: Oracle runs the control plane while you run node pools. Keep workers in private subnets, pull images through a NAT or service gateway, and expose services through OCI load balancers.

Compute shapes (flexible E4/E5, bare metal, dedicated hosts) trade cost against isolation. Block volumes and Object Storage (Standard vs Archive tiers) separate performance from durability - match the tier to how often the data is read.
