The OCI Architect Associate exam tests whether you can design solutions, not recite definitions. Every scenario here is a mini design decision — practice choosing between real options with trade-offs.
Track readiness per domain: 80%+ on scenario sets before moving on. The exam-prep domain at the end loops back to weak areas — plan for two passes, not one.

example.code: Week 1: start-here + IAM + networking. Week 2: compute + storage + database. Week 3: advanced domains + capstone. Week 4: exam-prep + mocks to 85%+.
example.walkthrough: Your 4-week arc: foundations, services, advanced, then prove it.

pitfalls: Skipping IAM — every later domain assumes it.
Reading without labs — the console builds intuition.
One pass instead of two — the second pass is where it sticks.
lessons.try_it: Take the systems-anatomy domain as a warm-up

lessons.title: Study Strategy for the OCI Architect Associate Exam
concepts: The exam blueprint weights: IAM/security, networking, compute, storage, database, and pricing/governance. Study proportionally — networking and IAM together are nearly a third of the exam.
Learn services in dependency order: regions/ADs -> IAM policies -> VCN -> compute -> storage -> database. Each layer's questions assume the previous layer's vocabulary.
For every service, know: what it's for, when to choose it over the alternative, one key limit, and the pricing dimension. 'When would you pick X over Y' is the exam's favorite question shape.
Build a personal 'service chooser' note as you go: one line per service (use case, key limit, pricing axis). Review it daily in week 4 — it's your whole exam on one page.

example.code: Service chooser line: 'Object Storage: unstructured blobs, 10GB... actually unlimited, priced per GB-month + requests; vs Block: boot/data volumes for instances.'
example.walkthrough: Start your service-chooser note with IAM and networking today.

pitfalls: Studying alphabetically instead of by blueprint weight.
Memorizing definitions without the X-vs-Y trade-off.
No single-page review note for the final week.
lessons.try_it: Write service-chooser lines for 5 core services

lessons.title: Course Roadmap Overview
concepts: Core domains (1-6): regions/ADs, compute, networking, storage, IAM/security, pricing/governance — the architect's foundation. These six are the exam's center of gravity.

Advanced domains (7-11): database services, containers/OKE, observability, backup/DR, plus exam-prep — the specialist layer that separates passing from excelling, and the capstone that proves you can build.
Capstone: design and deploy a 3-tier app (web, app, database) with proper networking, security, and cost controls. It's the portfolio piece — 'I built this on OCI' beats 'I studied OCI'.
Systems-anatomy runs alongside as your reference layer: how the pieces fit physically and logically. Consult it whenever a service's placement confuses you.

example.code: Core (6) -> Advanced (4) -> Capstone -> Exam-prep -> Mocks. Systems-anatomy alongside throughout as reference.
example.walkthrough: Map your experience to the roadmap — where's your weakest core domain?

pitfalls: Jumping to OKE before networking fundamentals.
lessons.try_it: Rate yourself 1-5 on each core domain

lessons.title: Terminal and Lab Guide for OCI
concepts: Labs use the OCI CLI and console against practice tenancies. The CLI pattern is always: oci <service> <resource> <action> --param value. Tab-complete and --help are your friends — never guess flag names.
Authentication: API keys in ~/.oci/config for the CLI; instance principals for workloads. Never paste tenancy OCIDs or keys into chat, tickets, or shared docs — they're credentials.
Lab hygiene: every lab names its compartment and tags resources (Project=capstone). Untagged experiments become surprise bills — the pricing domain will teach you why this matters.
The console's 'Copy as CLI' feature turns any console action into the equivalent CLI command — use it to learn CLI syntax from console clicks, then automate from there.

example.code: oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy-ocid> --query 'data[].{name:name}' --output table
example.walkthrough: List compartments as a table — your first CLI muscle memory.

pitfalls: Resources without tags or named compartments.
Sharing OCIDs/keys in tickets or chat.
lessons.try_it: Configure your CLI and list compartments

lessons.title: Phase 1: Network and Security Foundation
concepts: The capstone builds a 3-tier app: public web tier, private app tier, private database tier. Phase 1 creates the VCN with public/private subnets across two availability domains, an internet gateway, and a NAT gateway.

Security lists and NSGs: the web tier allows 443 from the internet; the app tier allows traffic only from the web NSG; the database tier allows 1521 only from the app NSG. Default-deny everywhere else — draw the matrix before creating anything.

IAM: a capstone compartment, a group for the project, and policies granting exactly the needed permissions (manage instances in the compartment, not the tenancy). Least privilege from the first resource.
Deliverable: a network diagram with CIDRs, gateways, route tables, and the security matrix — reviewed before any compute is launched. Architects draw first, click second.

example.code: oci network vcn create --compartment-id <c> --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 --display-name capstone-vcn
example.walkthrough: The VCN is the first resource — everything hangs off it.

pitfalls: One flat subnet for all tiers.
Security lists allowing 0.0.0.0/0 to the database.
Tenancy-wide IAM policies for a project.
lessons.try_it: Draw your 3-tier network diagram with CIDRs

lessons.title: Phase 2: Compute, Database, and Data
concepts: Phase 2 launches the tiers: an instance pool with autoscaling behind a public load balancer (web), private instances for the app tier, and an Autonomous Database (shared) for the data tier.

Database choice rationale: Autonomous Serverless for the capstone — auto-scaling, auto-patching, no DBA overhead. Document why not DB Systems (overkill) or HeatWave (wrong workload) — the exam loves 'why this service'.
Block volumes for app-tier data, object storage for static assets and backups. Each storage choice gets a one-line justification tied to access pattern — the habit the exam tests.
Health checks on the load balancer, backups enabled on the database from day one. Production habits in the capstone, not after.

example.code: oci db autonomous-database create --compartment-id <c> --db-name capdb --admin-password '<pw>' --cpu-core-count 1 --data-storage-size-in-tbs 1
example.walkthrough: Autonomous DB, 1 OCPU to start — scale when metrics say so.

pitfalls: Storage chosen by habit, not access pattern.
lessons.try_it: Write the service-choice rationale for each tier

lessons.title: Phase 3: Observability, Cost, and Hardening
concepts: Phase 3 makes it production-grade: monitoring alarms (CPU, error rate), log aggregation, a dashboard, and a monthly cost budget alarm. If you can't see it or price it, it's not production.
Hardening pass: rotate credentials into Vault, restrict security lists to the documented matrix, enable Cloud Guard, and verify no public buckets. The security review is a checklist, not a feeling.

Cost review: tag everything, check the cost analyzer, right-size the instance pool minimums, and set a budget alert at 80% of the monthly target. The pricing domain's lessons applied to your own build.
Deliverable: architecture diagram, cost estimate, security checklist sign-off, and a 5-minute demo. Present it like a design review — because that's what the exam's scenario questions simulate.

example.code: oci budgets budget create --compartment-id <c> --display-name capstone-monthly --amount 200 --reset-period MONTHLY
example.walkthrough: A $200 monthly budget with alerts — cost as a designed constraint.

pitfalls: Untagged resources in the cost report.
lessons.try_it: Define your capstone's monthly budget

lessons.title: Regions, Availability Domains, and Fault Domains
concepts: OCI regions are geographic areas with one or more availability domains (ADs); ADs are isolated data centers with independent power, cooling, and networking within a region. Design for AD failure, not just instance failure.

Fault domains are groupings within an AD that isolate hardware failures — spread instances across fault domains so a rack failure doesn't take your whole tier. Three fault domains per AD is the standard.
Realm concept: a realm is a logical collection of regions isolated from other realms (commercial vs government). Your tenancy lives in one realm; resources can't cross realm boundaries.
Choosing regions: latency to users first, then service availability (not every service is in every region), then data residency requirements. Multi-region is for DR and global latency, not a default.

example.code: oci iam region list --query 'data[].{name:name}' --output table
example.walkthrough: List all regions available to your tenancy — know your options before designing.

pitfalls: Assuming all services exist in all regions.
Ignoring fault domains within an AD.
lessons.try_it: List regions and note which has the lowest latency to you

lessons.title: Tenancy, Compartments, and Organization
concepts: The tenancy is your OCI account root — one per organization typically. Compartments are the isolation and billing boundaries inside it; design the compartment hierarchy before creating resources.
Compartment strategy: by environment (prod/dev/test), by team, or by project — pick one primary axis. Deep nesting (5+ levels) becomes unmanageable; 2-3 levels suits most orgs.
Compartments and IAM policies work together: policies grant permissions per compartment. A clean compartment tree makes least-privilege policies writable; a flat mess makes them impossible.
Deleting compartments requires them to be empty — plan the hierarchy deliberately because reorganizing later means moving every resource. Tags complement compartments for cost tracking.

example.code: oci iam compartment create --compartment-id <tenancy-ocid> --name prod --description 'Production workloads'
example.walkthrough: Create the prod compartment — the first organizational decision.

pitfalls: Dozens of flat compartments with no hierarchy.
Reorganizing compartments after hundreds of resources exist.
lessons.try_it: Sketch a 2-level compartment hierarchy for a startup

lessons.title: Service Limits and Quotas
concepts: Every OCI resource has service limits per AD/region/tenancy — compute OCPU counts, VCN counts, public IPs. Hitting a limit mid-deploy fails the whole plan; check limits during design, not during outage.
Request limit increases before you need them — approvals take time. Production launches should have limits raised 2x expected peak, not exactly at peak.
Quotas (compartment-level) let admins cap resource consumption per compartment — the cost-control companion to service limits. Set quotas on dev/test compartments aggressively.
Monitoring limits: the Limits page shows usage vs limit per service. Review it in the design phase and add it to the pre-launch checklist.

example.code: oci limits limit list --compartment-id <tenancy-ocid> --service-name compute --query 'data[?name==`standard-e4-count`]'
example.walkthrough: Check your compute OCPU limit before planning the instance pool.

pitfalls: Designing for 100 OCPUs with a 32-OCPU limit.
lessons.try_it: Check three service limits relevant to your capstone

lessons.title: Multi-AD and Multi-Region Design Patterns
concepts: Multi-AD pattern: spread web/app tiers across 2-3 ADs with a load balancer; data tier with replication. Survives AD failure — the standard production topology in a single region.

Multi-region pattern: active-passive (pilot light or warm standby in region B) or active-active (traffic split). Active-passive is cheaper and simpler; active-active needs data replication solved first.

Data is the hard part of multi-region: object storage cross-region copy, database Data Guard across regions, and the RPO/RTO math that justifies the cost. Compute is easy to replicate; consistent data is not.
Exam framing: 'needs to survive region failure' -> multi-region with replication; 'needs to survive AD failure' -> multi-AD. Match the pattern to the stated requirement, not the maximum possible.

example.code: oci network vcn create --compartment-id <c> --cidr-block 10.1.0.0/16 --display-name dr-vcn # region B
example.walkthrough: The DR region's VCN — same design, different region.

pitfalls: No RPO/RTO numbers driving the choice.
lessons.try_it: Choose multi-AD vs multi-region for 3 requirements

lessons.title: Shapes: VM, Bare Metal, and Specialty
concepts: Shapes define OCPU count, memory, and network bandwidth. VM shapes (E4, E5 flex) share physical hosts; bare metal gives the whole server — needed for licensed software, hypervisor control, or extreme performance.
Flex shapes let you pick OCPU and memory independently — the cost optimizer's shape. Fixed shapes are simpler but waste the ratio you don't need. Default to flex unless there's a reason not to.
Specialty shapes: GPU shapes for ML/HPC, HPC shapes with RDMA networking, burstable shapes for low-utilization workloads (credits accrue when idle). Match the shape to the workload's actual profile.
Shape changes require instance recreation or migration — pick carefully at design time. The exam tests 'which shape for X workload' constantly; workload profile -> shape is the mapping.

example.code: oci compute shape list --compartment-id <c> --query 'data[?contains(shape,`Flex`)].shape'
example.walkthrough: List flex shapes — your default choice for general workloads.

pitfalls: Bare metal for a stateless web tier.
Fixed shapes wasting the memory ratio.
GPU shapes for CPU-bound batch jobs.
lessons.try_it: Pick shapes for: web tier, ML training, nightly batch

lessons.title: Instance Pools and Autoscaling
concepts: Instance pools manage groups of identical instances: same shape, image, and config. The pool handles replacement of unhealthy instances — self-healing capacity.
Autoscaling policies: metric-based (CPU > 70% add instances), schedule-based (scale up at 8 AM), or both. Cooldown periods prevent flapping — scale decisions need time to take effect.
Pool + load balancer is the standard web-tier pattern: the pool provides elastic capacity, the LB distributes traffic and health-checks. Neither works well alone for production.
Health checks at the pool level replace failed instances automatically. Combined with multi-AD placement, the pool survives both instance and AD failures.

example.code: oci compute-management instance-pool create --compartment-id <c> --instance-configuration-id <ic> --size 2 --display-name web-pool
example.walkthrough: Create the pool — placement config spreads it across ADs.

pitfalls: Manual instance management for a spiky workload.
Pool without a load balancer for web traffic.
lessons.try_it: Design an autoscaling policy for 9-to-5 traffic

lessons.title: Custom Images and Instance Configuration
concepts: Custom images capture a configured instance (OS + software + config) for repeatable launches. Golden images make the pool's instances identical — no snowflake servers.
Instance configurations pair an image with shape and metadata — the pool's launch template. Update the config, then rolling-update the pool to refresh instances.
Image lifecycle: build in dev, test, promote to prod; version images (app-v1.2) and keep the last two. Unversioned 'latest' images make rollbacks guesswork.
Cloud-init/user-data scripts configure instances at boot — but bake stable config into the image and keep user-data for environment-specific bits (role, cluster join).

example.code: oci compute image create --compartment-id <c> --instance-id <i> --display-name app-v1.2
example.walkthrough: Capture the golden image — versioned, reproducible.

pitfalls: All config in user-data, nothing baked.
lessons.try_it: Define your image versioning scheme

lessons.title: Preemptible and Burstable Instances
concepts: Preemptible instances are spare capacity at a deep discount — reclaimable with notice. Perfect for fault-tolerant batch, CI runners, and dev/test. Never for the production database.
Design for preemption: stateless workers, checkpointed batch jobs, instance pools that replace reclaimed capacity. If your workload can't lose an instance anytime, it's not preemptible-eligible.
Burstable shapes accrue CPU credits when idle and burst when needed — ideal for low-average-utilization workloads (small web apps, dev servers). Sustained high CPU exhausts credits fast.
Cost math: preemptible can cut compute spend 50%+ for eligible workloads. The exam's cost-optimization questions love preemptible for batch/dev — know the eligibility rule cold.

example.code: oci compute instance launch --availability-domain <ad> --compartment-id <c> --shape VM.Standard.E4.Flex --preemptible true --display-name batch-worker
example.walkthrough: Launch a preemptible worker — cheap, losable, replaceable.

lessons.try_it: Classify 5 workloads as preemptible-eligible or not

lessons.title: OS Management and Patching
concepts: OS Management service patches and manages instance OSs fleet-wide: scheduled patch windows, package management, and compliance reporting. Unpatched instances are the #1 finding in every assessment.
Patch strategy: dev first, then staging, then prod — with rollback plans. Automated patching without staging is how outages happen; manual patching without automation is how drift happens.
The exam angle: 'instances must be patched with minimal effort' -> OS Management; 'no SSH access to instances' -> combine with bastion/session policies. Service-to-requirement mapping again.
Compliance reports show patch status per instance — feed them to your dashboard. Visibility drives patching; invisible instances stay vulnerable.

example.code: oci os-management-hub managed-instance list --compartment-id <c> --query 'data[].{name:"display-name"}'
example.walkthrough: List managed instances — the patch visibility baseline.

lessons.try_it: Design a 3-stage patch rollout

lessons.title: VCN, Subnets, and CIDR Planning
concepts: A VCN is your private network with a CIDR block you choose (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16). Subnets carve it up — public (internet-routed) or private (no internet route). CIDR planning is the first design act.
CIDR math: /16 gives 65K addresses; subnets like /24 give 254 usable. Reserve space: leave gaps between subnets for growth, and never overlap VCN CIDRs you plan to peer.
Subnet types: regional (recommended — spans ADs, survives AD failure) vs AD-specific (legacy). Default to regional subnets; AD-specific only for special pinning needs.
DNS in the VCN: private DNS views resolve instance hostnames internally. Plan DNS labels on subnets/VCNs — unnamed resources make troubleshooting miserable.

example.code: oci network subnet create --compartment-id <c> --vcn-id <v> --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 --display-name web-public --dns-label webpub
example.walkthrough: Create the public web subnet with a DNS label.

pitfalls: One /24 for everything — no growth room.
lessons.try_it: Plan CIDRs for a 3-tier VCN with growth room

lessons.title: Gateways: IGW, NAT, Service, DRG
concepts: Internet gateway: public subnet -> internet, inbound and outbound. NAT gateway: private subnet -> internet, outbound only. Service gateway: private access to OCI services (object storage) without internet exposure.
Dynamic routing gateway (DRG): connects VCNs to on-premises (IPsec VPN, FastConnect) and to other VCNs (remote peering). The hybrid-cloud front door.

Route tables direct traffic: public subnet routes 0.0.0.0/0 to the IGW; private routes 0.0.0.0/0 to NAT and the object-storage CIDR to the service gateway. Wrong routes are the #1 'can't reach X' cause.
Exam pattern: 'private instances need patches without internet' -> NAT or service gateway; 'on-prem connectivity' -> DRG with VPN/FastConnect. Requirement -> gateway mapping.

example.code: oci network nat-gateway create --compartment-id <c> --vcn-id <v> --display-name private-nat
example.walkthrough: NAT gateway for the private subnets' outbound patches.

pitfalls: IGW route on a private subnet.
DRG for VCN-to-VCN in the same region (use peering).
lessons.try_it: Choose gateways for 4 connectivity requirements

lessons.title: Security Lists vs NSGs
concepts: Security lists are subnet-level firewalls (all instances in the subnet); NSGs are instance-level (apply to specific VNICs across subnets). NSGs are the modern, precise tool — prefer them for tier-to-tier rules.
Stateful vs stateless: stateful rules auto-allow return traffic; stateless need explicit egress for responses. Default to stateful; stateless only for special cases (and remember the return rules).

The tier matrix: web NSG allows 443 from 0.0.0.0/0; app NSG allows app-port from web NSG only; DB NSG allows 1521 from app NSG only. Write the matrix before creating rules — architects document first.
Common exam trap: security list allows traffic but the OS firewall blocks it (or vice versa). Network security is two layers — check both when troubleshooting.

example.code: oci network nsg create --compartment-id <c> --vcn-id <v> --display-name app-tier-nsg
example.walkthrough: Create the app-tier NSG — rules come next.

lessons.try_it: Write the 3-tier security matrix

lessons.title: Load Balancers: Public, Private, and Health Checks
concepts: OCI load balancers distribute traffic across backends: public (internet-facing) or private (internal). Shape/bandwidth configurable — size to expected throughput, not maximum fantasy.

Listeners, backend sets, backends: the listener takes traffic (port 443), the backend set defines policy (round robin, least connections) and health checks, backends are the instances. Three concepts, one flow.
Health checks determine which backends receive traffic — HTTP checks against /health are standard. Unhealthy backends get no traffic; the LB is the availability mechanism, not just distribution.
SSL termination at the LB offloads crypto from instances; backend encryption continues behind it. Path-based routing sends /api to app backends, /static to others — one LB, many services.

example.code: oci network load-balancer create --compartment-id <c> --display-name web-lb --shape flexible --shape-details '{"minimumBandwidthInMbps":10,"maximumBandwidthInMbps":100}' --subnet-ids '["<public-subnet>"]'
example.walkthrough: Flexible LB, 10-100 Mbps — scales with actual traffic.

pitfalls: No health checks — traffic to dead backends.
Oversized fixed shapes for tiny traffic.
SSL terminated with plaintext backends unconsidered.
lessons.try_it: Design listener/backend-set topology for 2 services

lessons.title: VCN Peering and Transit Routing
concepts: Local peering: two VCNs in the same region, non-overlapping CIDRs, connected via peering gateways with route table entries both ways. Peering is non-transitive — A-B and B-C doesn't give A-C.
Remote peering: VCNs in different regions via DRGs. The DRG is the peering endpoint — one DRG per VCN, route tables pointing at it. Cross-region private connectivity without internet.
Transit routing: a hub VCN with the DRG routes traffic between spokes (or on-prem). Each spoke peers to the hub; hub route tables forward. Non-transitive peering made transitive through the hub.
CIDR discipline: peering requires non-overlapping CIDRs — the #1 peering failure. Plan a private address scheme (10.x per VCN) before the first VCN exists.

example.code: oci network local-peering-gateway create --compartment-id <c> --vcn-id <v1> --display-name to-vcn2
example.walkthrough: Peering gateway on VCN 1 — VCN 2 gets its mirror, routes both ways.

lessons.try_it: Design hub-and-spoke for 3 VCNs

lessons.title: Block Volumes: Performance and Backup
concepts: Block volumes are network-attached disks for instances: boot volumes and data volumes. Performance tiers (balanced, higher performance, ultra high) set IOPS/throughput — match to workload, not ego.
Volume groups snapshot related volumes together — crash-consistent backups for multi-volume apps (database + logs). Individual snapshots of related volumes can be inconsistent.
Backup policy: scheduled full + incremental block backups to object storage, with cross-region copy for DR. Test restores — untested backups are Schrödinger's backups.
Detaching and reattaching volumes moves data between instances — the recovery and migration primitive. Encrypted by default; customer-managed keys via Vault for compliance.

example.code: oci bv volume create --compartment-id <c> --availability-domain <ad> --size-in-gbs 100 --vpus-per-gb 20 --display-name app-data
example.walkthrough: 100GB, 20 VPUs/GB — performance chosen, not defaulted.

pitfalls: Individual snapshots of a DB + its logs.
No backup policy — 'we'll do it manually'.
lessons.try_it: Choose volume performance for 3 workloads

lessons.title: Object Storage: Tiers, Lifecycle, and Access
concepts: Object storage holds unstructured data as objects in buckets: Standard (hot), Infrequent Access (cooler), Archive (cold, slow retrieval). Lifecycle policies move objects down tiers automatically by age.
Access: private by default — pre-authenticated requests (PARs) grant temporary URL access without IAM accounts. Public buckets are occasionally right (static websites) but usually a finding.
Multipart upload for large objects; versioning protects against overwrites; retention rules enforce compliance holds. Each feature answers a specific requirement — know which.
Pricing axes: storage GB-months, requests, and data transfer. Archive is cheap to store, expensive to retrieve — lifecycle policies must match actual access patterns.

example.code: oci os bucket create --compartment-id <c> --name app-assets --public-access-type NoPublicAccess
example.walkthrough: Private bucket — public is the exception, never the default.

pitfalls: Archive tier for frequently accessed objects.
No lifecycle policy — hot storage forever.
lessons.try_it: Design lifecycle policy for logs (hot 30d, archive after)

lessons.title: File Storage (FSS) and Use Cases
concepts: File Storage provides NFS shares for multiple instances — the shared-filesystem answer. Mount targets in the VCN, exports with CIDR-restricted access. Web server farms sharing uploads is the classic case.
When FSS vs block vs object: shared POSIX access across instances -> FSS; single-instance disk -> block; unstructured HTTP access -> object. The exam tests this three-way choice directly.
Snapshots of file systems for point-in-time recovery; replication for DR. Performance: throughput scales with usage — understand the billing (used capacity, not provisioned).
Security: export options restrict which CIDRs mount with what permissions (read/write vs read-only). Open exports are a finding — scope them like security lists.

example.code: oci fs file-system create --compartment-id <c> --availability-domain <ad> --display-name shared-uploads
example.walkthrough: File system for the web farm's shared uploads.

pitfalls: Object storage for POSIX file locking.
lessons.try_it: Choose FSS/block/object for 5 scenarios

lessons.title: Data Transfer and Migration
concepts: Online transfer: CLI/API uploads, multipart for large files. Offline: Data Transfer Service — ship physical disks/appliances for petabyte-scale seeding. The 100TB-over-the-wire math decides.
Transfer math: 100 TB at 1 Gbps takes ~10 days (and that's perfect conditions). The exam loves 'how to get 500TB into OCI fastest' — the answer is usually the offline appliance.
Migration pattern: seed offline (appliance), then incremental online sync for the delta, cutover during the window. Two-phase migration minimizes downtime and risk.
Checksums and verification: every transfer verifies integrity (MD5 per object). Unverified transfers are corrupted transfers you haven't discovered yet.

example.code: oci os object bulk-upload --bucket-name seed --src-dir /data/seed --parallel-operations 8
example.walkthrough: Parallel bulk upload — the online path for moderate data.

pitfalls: 500TB over a 1 Gbps link 'over the weekend'.
lessons.try_it: Compute transfer time for 50TB at 500 Mbps

lessons.title: Storage Security and Encryption
concepts: Encryption at rest is default (Oracle-managed keys); Vault brings customer-managed keys with rotation and revocation. Compliance requirements dictate which — know the control difference.
Access control: IAM policies on buckets, PARs for temporary access, and no public buckets by default. Audit public buckets regularly — they appear via accidents, not plans.
Private endpoints keep storage traffic off the internet (service gateway / private endpoint). Data in transit uses TLS; private routing removes the internet path entirely.
Retention and legal holds: object retention rules prevent deletion for compliance periods. Configure before the audit, not during — retention can't be retroactively applied to deleted data.

example.code: oci kms management vault create --compartment-id <c> --display-name storage-keys
example.walkthrough: Vault for customer-managed storage keys.

pitfalls: Oracle-managed keys for strict compliance needs.
No retention rules before the compliance audit.
lessons.try_it: Decide key management for 3 compliance levels

lessons.title: Users, Groups, and Compartments
concepts: IAM users are humans (or break-glass); groups collect users; policies grant group permissions on compartments. Never attach policies to users directly — groups are the indirection that scales.
Compartment design and IAM are one decision: policies reference compartments, so the compartment tree IS the permission boundary map. Design them together.
Break-glass admin: one emergency user with MFA, credentials sealed, usage alerted. Regular admin work happens through federated groups — the break-glass is for IdP outages only.
Policy verbs: inspect < read < use < manage — each includes the previous. Grant the minimum verb that works; 'manage' when 'read' suffices is the classic over-grant.

example.code: oci iam group create --compartment-id <tenancy> --name app-admins --description 'App team admins'
example.walkthrough: Group first — policies attach to groups, never users.

lessons.try_it: Map verbs to 4 team roles

lessons.title: Policy Syntax Deep Dive
concepts: Policy grammar: Allow group <name> to <verb> <resource> in compartment <name> [where <conditions>]. Every policy is this sentence — learn to read and write it fluently.
Conditions narrow policies: where target.tag = 'Project=capstone', where request.region = 'us-ashburn-1'. Conditions turn broad verbs into precise permissions.

Common patterns: instance-principal policies (allow dynamic-group webservers to read objects in compartment assets), end-user self-management (allow group users to manage api-keys in tenancy where target.user = request.user).
Troubleshooting: 'not authorized' means no matching Allow — check group membership, compartment path, verb coverage, and conditions. The policy simulator (or careful reading) beats guessing.

example.code: oci iam policy create --compartment-id <c> --name web-read-assets --statements '["Allow dynamic-group webservers to read objects in compartment assets"]' --description 'Web tier reads static assets'
example.walkthrough: Dynamic group + read-only objects — least privilege for the web tier.

pitfalls: Allow group X to manage all-resources in tenancy.
Guessing at 'not authorized' instead of reading.
lessons.try_it: Write 3 policies: dev read, app manage-in-compartment, auditor inspect

lessons.title: Dynamic Groups and Instance Principals
concepts: Dynamic groups match instances by rules (compartment, tag): instances get IAM permissions without embedded credentials. The web tier reads Object Storage as itself, not as a hardcoded user.
Matching rules: ALL {instance.compartment.id = '<ocid>'} or tag-based. Test rules with the 'matching instances' preview — wrong rules silently grant nothing (or everything, if too broad).
Instance principals: code on the instance calls OCI APIs authenticated as the instance. No API keys to rotate, leak, or manage — the credential problem disappears by design.
Use cases: instances reading buckets, writing logs, calling functions. Any workload-to-OCI-API call should use instance principals; API keys on instances are the finding.

example.code: oci iam dynamic-group create --compartment-id <tenancy> --name webservers --matching-rule "ALL {instance.compartment.id = '<c>'}" --description 'Web tier instances'
example.walkthrough: Dynamic group matching the web compartment's instances.

pitfalls: API keys baked into instance images.
lessons.try_it: Design dynamic-group rules for 3 tiers

lessons.title: MFA, Federation, and Identity
concepts: MFA: enforce for all human users, especially admins — password-only admins are the breach headline. TOTP apps or security keys; SMS as the weakest fallback.
Federation: IdP (Okta, Azure AD) -> OCI IAM mapping groups. Users authenticate at the IdP; OCI trusts the SAML assertion. One identity lifecycle, managed once.
Group mapping: IdP groups map to OCI groups — 'Cloud-Admins' in the IdP becomes OCI admin powers. Review mappings regularly; stale mappings are privilege creep.
API key hygiene: rotate regularly, scope to need, delete unused. Keys are the non-human credential — inventory them like you inventory instances.

example.code: oci iam mfa-totp-device create --user-id <user-ocid> --seed <seed>
example.walkthrough: Enroll the TOTP device — MFA for every human.

lessons.try_it: Audit MFA coverage and API key age

lessons.title: Cloud Guard, Security Zones, and Vault
concepts: Cloud Guard: the security posture monitor — detectors (config, activity, threat) + responders (auto-remediate or notify). Enable it on day one; it's the fleet-wide security camera.
Security zones: compartments with enforced policies (no public buckets, no open DB ports) — guardrails that reject violating resources at creation. Prevention beats detection.

Vault: secrets (passwords, API keys) and encryption keys with rotation, versioning, and audit. Application credentials live in Vault; instance principals fetch them at runtime — never in code or metadata.
The triad: Cloud Guard watches, Security Zones prevent, Vault holds secrets. Together they're the 'secure by default' story — know which does what for the exam.

example.code: oci secrets secret-bundle create --secret-id <s> --payload-content '<base64>' --description 'DB password rotation'
example.walkthrough: Store the DB password in Vault — never in metadata.

pitfalls: No security zones on prod compartments.
lessons.try_it: Map 5 security requirements to Guard/Zones/Vault

lessons.title: Pricing Models and Dimensions
concepts: OCI pricing dimensions: OCPU-hours, GB-months, requests, data transfer. Every service bills on 1-3 axes — the service-chooser note records each service's axes.
Pay-as-you-go vs committed: monthly flex (discount for committing spend) and annual commitments trade flexibility for price. Steady workloads commit; spiky ones stay PAYG.
Always Free tier: real resources (instances, databases, storage) free forever within limits — the lab and dev answer. Know the Always Free boundaries; exceeding them bills normally.
Data transfer: ingress free, egress metered (with a generous free allowance). Architectures that chat across regions pay the egress tax — keep data local when possible.

example.code: oci budgets budget create --compartment-id <c> --display-name monthly-cap --amount 500 --reset-period MONTHLY --description 'Hard monthly ceiling'
example.walkthrough: Budget with alerts — the governance backstop.

pitfalls: Ignoring the pricing axes when choosing services.
lessons.try_it: Compute monthly cost for your capstone design

lessons.title: Cost Analysis and Tagging
concepts: Cost Analysis shows spend by compartment, tag, service, and time — the 'where did the money go' tool. Tag-driven analysis requires tags applied at creation; retroactive tagging is archaeology.
Tagging strategy: defined tags (managed keys: Project, Environment, Owner) beat freeform tags (typos create parallel universes). Enforce via tag defaults and namespace rules.
Top cost drivers are usually: oversized instances, unattached block volumes, old snapshots, and Always-On dev resources. The monthly review hunts these four first.
Showback: tag-based cost reports per team/project make spend visible to owners. Invisible costs grow; attributed costs get optimized.

example.code: oci iam tag-namespace create --compartment-id <tenancy> --name CostTracking --description 'Mandatory cost tags'
example.walkthrough: Tag namespace first — freeform tags come later, if ever.

lessons.try_it: Define 4 mandatory tags for your org

lessons.title: Budgets, Alerts, and Quotas
concepts: Budgets: set spend thresholds per compartment/tag with alert rules (80% actual, 100% forecast). Alerts go to email/topics — someone must own the response, or alerts are theater.
Quotas: hard caps on resource counts per compartment (max 10 OCPUs in dev). Budgets warn; quotas enforce. Dev/test gets quotas; prod gets budgets with on-call response.
Anomaly detection: sudden spend spikes trigger investigation — usually a misconfigured autoscaling policy or a forgotten load test. The alert is the start, not the end.
Governance rhythm: weekly automated review, monthly human review, quarterly commitment optimization. Cadence turns cost control from project into habit.

example.code: oci quotas quota create --compartment-id <dev-c> --name dev-ocpu-cap --statements '["zero compute quotas in dev except 8 standard cores"]' --description 'Dev OCPU ceiling'
example.walkthrough: Quota the dev compartment — hard ceiling, no surprises.

lessons.try_it: Set budget + quota for a dev compartment

lessons.title: Licensing: BYOL and Included
concepts: BYOL (bring your own license): apply existing Oracle licenses to OCI (DB, WebLogic) for credit — the license-mobility answer for enterprises with Oracle estates. Requires license compliance verification.
License-included: hourly price bundles the license — simpler, no existing licenses needed. Compare BYOL vs included on total cost for your license position; the answer differs per org.
Database licensing is the big one: Autonomous includes the license options question (which packs are enabled); DB Systems have BYOL vs included shapes. Get this wrong and the bill doubles.
Exam angle: 'company has Oracle DB licenses' -> BYOL; 'startup, no licenses' -> included. The stem states the license position — the answer follows directly.

example.code: Comparison: existing EE licenses + BYOL Autonomous = license cost avoided; startup with no licenses = included hourly. The stem's license position decides.
example.walkthrough: BYOL vs included follows the license inventory — read the stem.

pitfalls: Included pricing when BYOL licenses exist.
lessons.try_it: Choose BYOL vs included for 3 org profiles

lessons.title: Governance: Policies, Audit, and Compliance
concepts: Audit service: every API call logged, immutable, searchable — the 'who did what' record. Retain per compliance needs; the audit log is the first artifact in any incident.
IAM policies as governance: least-privilege by default, regular access reviews, no standing admin. Policy changes themselves go through the audit log — governance watches the governors.
Compliance frameworks map to OCI controls: encryption (Vault), network isolation (security zones), logging (Audit + Logging), access control (IAM). Know the mapping for regulated workloads.

Landing zone: the opinionated starting setup (compartments, IAM, network, logging, budgets) — deploy it first, customize after. Greenfield tenancies without a landing zone accumulate debt from day one.

example.code: oci audit event list --compartment-id <tenancy> --start-time 2026-10-01T00:00:00Z --query 'data[?contains("action-name",`Delete`)]'
example.walkthrough: Audit the deleters — who removed what this month.

pitfalls: Audit log retention shorter than compliance needs.
No landing zone — organic tenancy sprawl.
lessons.try_it: Map 4 compliance needs to OCI controls

lessons.title: Autonomous Database: ATP and ADW
concepts: Autonomous Database comes in transaction processing (ATP) and data warehouse (ADW) flavors — same automation (self-patching, self-tuning), different workload optimization. OLTP vs analytics is the choice.

Serverless vs dedicated: serverless shares infrastructure and scales instantly (the elastic answer); dedicated (Exadata) gives isolated hardware for performance/noisy-neighbor needs. Cost follows isolation.
Auto-scaling: OCPU scales up automatically within limits during load spikes — set the max and forget. The exam's 'variable workload, minimal admin' answer is almost always Autonomous serverless.
Connection: wallets for secure connectivity (mTLS), connection strings per service level (high/medium/low parallelism). Wallet rotation is the credential hygiene for ATP/ADW.

example.code: oci db autonomous-database list --compartment-id <c> --query 'data[].{name:"display-name",type:"db-workload"}'
example.walkthrough: List Autonomous DBs with their workload type — ATP or ADW at a glance.

pitfalls: Dedicated Exadata for a 10GB dev database.
lessons.try_it: Choose ATP vs ADW for 4 workloads

lessons.title: DB Systems: VM and Bare Metal
concepts: DB Systems run Oracle Database on VM or bare metal shapes you manage — you patch, you tune, you back up (with tooling help). Control in exchange for labor; the opposite of Autonomous.
When DB Systems over Autonomous: specific version needs, custom extensions, Data Guard configurations Autonomous doesn't offer, or license/BYOL strategies tied to DB Systems.
VM vs bare metal DB: VM for standard workloads (flex shapes, easy scaling); bare metal for extreme performance or dense consolidation. Two-node RAC available on both for HA.
Storage: ASM-managed, performance scales with the shape; backups to object storage with the console-managed backup service. Patching is your calendar item — schedule it.

example.code: oci db system list --compartment-id <c> --query 'data[].{name:"display-name",shape:shape}'
example.walkthrough: List DB systems and their shapes — your managed fleet.

pitfalls: DB Systems when Autonomous fits (paying admin tax).
No patch calendar for managed DBs.
lessons.try_it: Decide Autonomous vs DB System for 4 cases

lessons.title: MySQL HeatWave and NoSQL
concepts: MySQL HeatWave: MySQL service with an in-memory analytics accelerator — transactions and analytics on one MySQL, no ETL. The 'MySQL that also does OLAP' answer.
When HeatWave: MySQL-compatible apps needing real-time analytics; lakehouse features for object-storage data. When not: pure OLTP at small scale (regular MySQL service suffices).
NoSQL Database Cloud: key-value/document store for high-velocity, flexible-schema workloads (sessions, catalogs, IoT). Throughput provisioned in read/write units — scale to the workload.
The exam's database-choice questions: relational + autonomous -> ATP; analytics -> ADW; MySQL -> HeatWave; key-value flexible -> NoSQL. Workload shape decides.

example.code: oci mysql db-system list --compartment-id <c> --query 'data[].{name:"display-name",heatwave:"heat-wave-cluster"}'
example.walkthrough: List MySQL systems and HeatWave enablement.

pitfalls: HeatWave for a pure key-value workload.
Ignoring the analytics accelerator for mixed workloads.
lessons.try_it: Map 5 workloads to the right OCI database

lessons.title: Data Guard and High Availability
concepts: Data Guard: standby database replicating from primary — automatic failover (with FSFO) or manual switchover. The RPO~0 Oracle HA answer; the exam's 'zero data loss' requirement points here.
Autonomous Data Guard: one-click standby in another AD or region — cross-region for DR. Serverless makes standby setup trivial compared to manual Data Guard.

RAC (Real Application Clusters): multiple instances on one database — scale-out and node-failure survival. RAC is HA within a data center; Data Guard is HA across them. Different failures, different tools.
Switchover vs failover: switchover is planned (no data loss, roles reverse); failover is emergency (possible data loss). Test both before the outage — untested DR is a hope, not a plan.

example.code: oci db data-guard-association list --database-id <db> --query 'data[].{role:role,lifecycle:"lifecycle-state"}'
example.walkthrough: Check Data Guard associations and their roles.

pitfalls: No standby for a zero-RPO requirement.
lessons.try_it: Choose RAC vs Data Guard for 3 requirements

lessons.title: Backups, PITR, and Clones
concepts: Autonomous backups: automatic, retained per policy, point-in-time recovery to any 5-minute window in retention. PITR is the 'oops' button — know the retention period for your tier.
Manual backups and long-term retention: keep specific backups beyond auto-retention for compliance. Tag them; compliance artifacts need findability.
Clones: full or metadata clones for dev/test — thin clones share storage, provisioning in minutes. Refresh dev from prod safely: clone, mask sensitive data, hand to developers.
Backup verification: restore tests on a schedule. The backup exists when the restore works — calendar the test, document the result.

example.code: oci db autonomous-database-backup list --compartment-id <c> --autonomous-database-id <db> --query 'data[].{time:"time-started",type:type}'
example.walkthrough: List backups with timestamps and types — the recovery inventory.

pitfalls: Assuming backups work without restore tests.
Prod data in dev without masking.
lessons.try_it: Define backup + clone policy for dev/test

lessons.title: Connecting Apps and Security
concepts: Connectivity: private endpoints for in-VCN access (no internet path), wallets for mTLS, connection pooling via the service levels. Private + wallet is the production pattern.
Database Vault and auditing: who accessed what, when. Enable auditing on sensitive schemas; the audit trail is the compliance artifact and the incident-response record.
Credential rotation: wallet passwords, admin passwords — rotate on schedule and on personnel changes. Vault-managed secrets with rotation policies automate this.
Network isolation: database in private subnet, NSG allowing 1521 only from app tier. Public database endpoints are the finding — the exam will show you one and expect you to flag it.

example.code: oci db autonomous-database generate-wallet --autonomous-database-id <db> --file wallet.zip --password '<pw>'
example.walkthrough: Generate the wallet — mTLS credentials for the app tier.

lessons.try_it: Harden a database's connectivity end to end

lessons.title: Container Instances: Serverless Containers
concepts: Container Instances run containers without managing hosts or Kubernetes — specify image, resources, done. The 'I just need this container running' answer; the exam contrasts it with OKE.

When Container Instances vs OKE: single/few containers, batch jobs, event-driven tasks -> Container Instances; orchestrated microservices needing service mesh/autoscaling -> OKE. Complexity follows need.
No cluster to patch, no nodes to size — serverless operations. But also no Kubernetes API, no advanced scheduling. The trade-off is control vs simplicity.
Pricing: per-second resource consumption. Idle containers cost nothing — the batch/event answer that beats always-on instances.

example.code: oci container-instances container-instance create --compartment-id <c> --availability-domain <ad> --display-name job-runner --containers '[{"image-url":"<image>","display-name":"job"}]'
example.walkthrough: Launch a serverless container — no cluster required.

pitfalls: OKE cluster for a single nightly batch job.
lessons.try_it: Choose Container Instances vs OKE for 4 workloads

lessons.title: OKE Clusters and Node Pools
concepts: OKE (Oracle Container Engine for Kubernetes): managed control plane, you manage worker node pools. Enhanced clusters add more features (virtual nodes, add-ons); basic clusters are simpler and cheaper.
Node pools: groups of worker nodes with shape, image, and size — autoscaling node pools grow with pod demand (cluster autoscaler). Separate pools per workload type (general, GPU, memory-heavy).
Virtual nodes: serverless Kubernetes workers — pods without node management, per-pod billing. Bursty or irregular workloads skip node sizing entirely.
Network: VCN-native pod networking (each pod gets a VCN IP) vs flannel overlay. VCN-native integrates with NSGs and observability — the enterprise answer; flannel is simpler for small clusters.

example.code: oci ce cluster list --compartment-id <c> --query 'data[].{name:name,type:type}'
example.walkthrough: List clusters and their types — basic vs enhanced at a glance.

pitfalls: One node pool for all workload types.
Manual node sizing for bursty workloads.
Flannel when VCN-native features are needed.
lessons.try_it: Design node pools for mixed workloads

lessons.title: Deployments, Services, and Ingress on OKE
concepts: Deployments manage replica sets of pods; Services give stable endpoints (ClusterIP internal, LoadBalancer external via OCI LB); Ingress routes HTTP paths/hosts to services — the standard traffic stack.
OCI LB integration: Service type LoadBalancer provisions an OCI load balancer automatically; Ingress controllers (nginx) run in-cluster for path-based routing. Know which creates cloud resources.
Health probes (liveness/readiness) keep traffic off broken pods — the Kubernetes equivalent of LB health checks. Missing probes mean traffic to dead pods.
Resource requests/limits per container: requests for scheduling, limits for protection. Unset limits let one pod starve the node — the noisy-neighbor finding in every cluster audit.

example.code: kubectl get deployments,svc,ingress -A
example.walkthrough: The traffic stack at a glance — deployments, services, ingress.

pitfalls: No health probes on web deployments.
lessons.try_it: Define probes and limits for a web deployment

lessons.title: Container Registry (OCIR) and Image Security
concepts: OCIR stores container images privately per region; replicate across regions for multi-region deploys. Private by default — public images are the exception with a reason.
Image scanning: vulnerability scanning on push — fail the pipeline on critical CVEs. Unsigned/unscanned images don't deploy to prod; the admission policy enforces it.
Image signing and policies: sign trusted images, enforce signature verification in-cluster. Supply-chain security is the exam's container-security angle — know the controls.
Lifecycle: tag immutably (sha or version, not just latest), prune old images, replicate per region. 'Latest' in prod is undeployable rollback roulette.

example.code: oci artifacts container repository list --compartment-id <c> --query 'data[]."display-name"'
example.walkthrough: List image repos — the supply-chain inventory.

lessons.try_it: Define image promotion policy dev->prod

lessons.title: OKE Networking and Security
concepts: Pod security: run as non-root, read-only filesystems, drop capabilities — the container hardening baseline. PodSecurity standards enforce it cluster-wide.
Network policies: default-deny between namespaces, explicit allow for required flows. Microsegmentation for pods — the same matrix thinking as NSGs, one level down.
Secrets: never in env vars in plain YAML — use OCI Vault via the secrets store CSI driver or sealed secrets. Etcd encryption for secrets at rest.
RBAC: least-privilege service accounts per workload; no cluster-admin for apps. Audit cluster-admin bindings regularly — they're the finding.

example.code: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:web:web-sa | head -20
example.walkthrough: Audit what the web service account can actually do.

lessons.try_it: Harden a namespace: policies, secrets, RBAC

lessons.title: Observability for Container Workloads
concepts: Container logs: stdout/stderr collected per pod, shipped to OCI Logging — no SSH into containers to read logs. Centralized logging from day one of the cluster.
Metrics: OKE cluster metrics (node/pod CPU/memory) in Monitoring; Prometheus for app metrics. Alarms on pod restarts, resource pressure, and failed deployments.
Tracing: distributed tracing across microservices — the latency debugging tool for service meshes. When the request is slow, the trace shows which hop.
The exam angle: 'containers crashing, why' -> logs + events (kubectl get events); 'slow requests' -> traces; 'node pressure' -> metrics + alarms. Symptom -> tool mapping.

example.code: kubectl logs -l app=web --tail=100 --prefix
example.walkthrough: Tail web pod logs with pod prefixes — the first debug step.

pitfalls: No alarms on pod crash loops.
lessons.try_it: Set up log shipping + 3 alarms for a cluster

lessons.title: Monitoring: Metrics and Namespaces
concepts: OCI Monitoring collects metrics in namespaces: oci_computeagent (CPU, memory), oci_lbaas (load balancer), oci_blockstore, and custom namespaces you publish. Namespace + metric + dimensions = the queryable unit.
Metric queries use MQL: CpuUtilization[1m].mean() grouped by resource. Learn the query pattern — alarms, dashboards, and autoscaling all consume the same queries.
Custom metrics: publish application metrics (orders/min, queue depth) via the API/CLI. Business metrics detect 'running but not working' — infrastructure metrics can't.
Resolution and retention: raw points for days, rollups longer. Design metric cardinality carefully — high-cardinality dimensions explode cost and slow queries.

example.code: oci monitoring metric-data summarize-metrics-data --compartment-id <c> --namespace oci_computeagent --query-name CpuUtilization --start-time 2026-10-10T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-10-10T01:00:00Z
example.walkthrough: Query CPU metrics for the last hour — MQL in the CLI.

pitfalls: Monitoring only infra metrics, not business metrics.
lessons.try_it: Publish one custom business metric

lessons.title: Alarms and Notifications
concepts: Alarms evaluate metric queries on an interval and fire when thresholds breach: critical (page), warning (ticket), info. Each alarm needs a defined responder — alarms without owners are noise.
Alarm anatomy: query, threshold, consecutive breaches (avoid single-spike pages), notification topic, and runbook link. The runbook link turns a page into an action.
Composite alarms: combine signals (high error rate AND low healthy backends) to page only on real incidents. Single-metric alarms page on noise; composites page on truth.
Notification topics fan out to email, PagerDuty, Slack, Functions. Test the whole chain — an alarm that can't notify is a dashboard decoration.

example.code: oci monitoring alarm create --compartment-id <c> --display-name 5xx-spike --metric-compartment-id <c> --namespace oci_lbaas --query 'HttpStatusCode500[1m].sum() > 10' --severity CRITICAL --destinations '["<topic>"]'
example.walkthrough: Alarm on 5xx spikes — user-impact paging.

lessons.try_it: Design alarms for a web service's SLOs

lessons.title: Logging and Log Search
concepts: OCI Logging aggregates: audit logs, service logs (LB, WAF, functions), and custom application logs. Enable logging per resource — it's not automatic everywhere.
Log groups organize logs; log search queries across them with a SQL-like language. Save useful queries — 'show me 5xx by backend' becomes a dashboard panel and an incident tool.
Retention and archival: hot search for recent, object storage archival for compliance. Log volume is the cost lever — filter noise at the source, not after ingestion.
The exam angle: 'troubleshoot failed requests' -> service logs + search; 'who deleted the instance' -> audit logs. Log type follows the question.

example.code: oci logging-search search-logs --search-query 'search "<log-group>/" | where data.status = 500 | timestats count by data.backend'
example.walkthrough: Count 500s by backend — the incident query.

pitfalls: Debug volume ingested at prod cost.
Audit logs confused with app logs.
lessons.try_it: Write 3 incident log queries

lessons.title: Events and Functions Automation
concepts: Events service emits state changes (instance launched, bucket created, alarm fired); rules match patterns and route to Functions, notifications, or streaming. The automation nervous system.
Rule anatomy: condition (event type + filters), action (function/topic/stream). 'On instance terminate, snapshot boot volume' is condition + function — declarative remediation.
Functions are serverless compute for the response: small, fast, idempotent. Keep them idempotent — events can deliver twice, and double-snapshots beat missed ones.
Common automations: tag enforcement on creation, backup on termination, Slack alerts on critical alarms, auto-remediation of guard findings. Each is a rule + function pair.

example.code: oci events rule create --compartment-id <c> --display-name snap-on-terminate --condition '{"eventType":["com.oraclecloud.computeapi.terminateinstance.end"]}' --actions '{"actions":[{"actionType":"FAAS","functionId":"<fn>"}]}'
example.walkthrough: Rule: on instance terminate, invoke the snapshot function.

pitfalls: Polling cron instead of event rules.
No automation for repeated manual responses.
lessons.try_it: Automate one repeated operational response

lessons.title: Health Checks and Status
concepts: Health Checks probe endpoints from multiple vantage points (regions) — external uptime monitoring independent of your infrastructure. If your region dies, the health check still reports.
Checks: HTTP/HTTPS/ping with assertions on status code, body content, and latency. Alert when assertions fail from N vantage points — one vantage point is noise, consensus is signal.
Status pages consume health checks: public or internal status derived from the same probes. The incident communication and the detection share a source of truth.
Combine with LB health checks: external (Health Checks service) verifies user-visible uptime; internal (LB) routes around failures. Two layers, two purposes.

example.code: oci health-checks http-monitor create --compartment-id <c> --display-name homepage --targets '["https://example.com"]' --protocol HTTPS --port 443
example.walkthrough: External HTTPS monitor from multiple regions.

pitfalls: Only internal health checks (blind to region failure).
Status page updated manually during incidents.
lessons.try_it: Set up external monitors for 3 endpoints

lessons.title: Dashboards and Incident Practice
concepts: Dashboards: curate per audience — exec (SLOs), on-call (signals + runbook links), service owners (their metrics). One dashboard per question, not one dashboard for everything.
Widget discipline: each chart answers one question ('is checkout healthy?'). Vanity charts (total requests ever) waste space; signal charts (error budget burn) drive action.

Incident practice: the dashboard is the incident interface — during a drill, navigate from alert to dashboard to logs to fix using only the linked artifacts. Gaps found in drills get fixed before incidents.
Review cadence: dashboards rot as services change. Quarterly dashboard review — remove dead charts, add new SLOs, verify runbook links.

example.code: oci monitoring dashboard create --compartment-id <c> --display-name checkout-slo --widgets '[{"title":"Error budget","query":"..."}]'
example.walkthrough: SLO dashboard skeleton — fill with the real queries.

lessons.try_it: Sketch the on-call dashboard for your capstone

lessons.title: RPO, RTO, and the DR Conversation
concepts: RPO (recovery point objective): how much data you can lose, in time. RTO (recovery time objective): how long you can be down. Every DR design starts with these two numbers — without them, you're guessing at cost.

Cost follows the numbers: RPO 0 + RTO minutes = synchronous replication + automation (expensive); RPO 24h + RTO 8h = nightly backups + manual restore (cheap). The business sets the numbers; engineering prices them.
Tiers: not every workload gets the same RPO/RTO. Tier 1 (minutes) vs Tier 3 (days) — tiering focuses DR spend where it matters. Uniform DR is uniformly wasteful.
Document the RPO/RTO per workload and get sign-off. The DR plan's first page is the numbers table — everything after is implementation of those numbers.

example.code: Numbers table: Orders DB: RPO 5min / RTO 30min (Tier 1). Analytics: RPO 24h / RTO 4h (Tier 2). Dev: RPO n/a / RTO best-effort (Tier 3).
example.walkthrough: Tier the workloads before designing anything.

pitfalls: Same DR tier for every workload.
lessons.try_it: Write RPO/RTO numbers for 3 workloads

lessons.title: Backup Strategies on OCI
concepts: OCI backup primitives: boot/block volume backups (full + incremental, to object storage), database automatic backups, object versioning. Each resource type has its native mechanism — use it.
3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 offsite. On OCI: production + automated backup + cross-region copy = 3-2-1 without tape. Cross-region copy is the offsite leg.
Backup policies: scheduled, tagged, with retention matching compliance. Manual backups before changes (pre-deploy snapshots) complement the schedule — automation plus judgment.
The exam's backup questions: 'survive region failure' -> cross-region copy; 'accidental deletion' -> versioning/PITR; 'compliance 7 years' -> long-term retention. Requirement -> mechanism.

example.code: oci bv backup create --volume-id <v> --type FULL --display-name pre-deploy-snap
example.walkthrough: Pre-deploy snapshot — the manual complement to scheduled policy.

pitfalls: No cross-region copy for regional DR needs.
lessons.try_it: Design backup policy for a 3-tier app

lessons.title: Cross-Region Copy and Replication
concepts: Cross-region copy for block backups and objects: async replication to a second region. RPO = copy interval; automate the copy, monitor its lag — unmonitored replication is a hope.
Object storage replication policies: whole-bucket replication with destination region and prefix filters. Versioning on both ends; the replica is independently readable.
Database cross-region Data Guard: the RPO~0 option for the data tier. Compute and network rebuild from IaC/templates in the DR region — data replicates, infrastructure re-deploys.
Failover DNS: health checks + DNS failover route users to the DR region. The data path and the traffic path fail over together — test both, not just one.

example.code: oci bv backup copy --volume-backup-id <b> --destination-region us-chicago-1 --display-name dr-copy
example.walkthrough: Copy the backup to the DR region — the offsite leg.

lessons.try_it: Map each tier to its replication mechanism

lessons.title: Pilot Light, Warm Standby, Active-Active
concepts: DR patterns by cost: backup-and-restore (cheapest, slowest), pilot light (core data replicated, infra on-demand), warm standby (scaled-down live copy), active-active (full dual run, fastest, priciest).
Pilot light detail: data replicates continuously; compute/network IaC deploys on failover. RTO = deploy time + data catch-up. The sweet spot for most Tier-1-but-not-critical workloads.
Warm standby: minimal live infra in DR region (small instance pool, read replica DB), scaled up on failover. RTO in minutes; cost is the idle footprint. DNS failover completes the picture.
Choose by RTO: hours -> backup/restore; <1h -> pilot light; minutes -> warm standby; ~0 -> active-active. The RTO number from lesson 1 selects the pattern mechanically.

example.code: Selection: RTO 4h -> pilot light (data replicates, IaC on failover). RTO 10min -> warm standby. RTO 0 -> active-active with sync replication.
example.walkthrough: RTO selects the pattern — it's mechanical, not stylistic.

pitfalls: Warm standby cost for a 24h-RTO workload.
Pilot light without IaC for the infra rebuild.
lessons.try_it: Select DR patterns for 4 RTO requirements

lessons.title: Testing the DR Plan
concepts: Untested DR is fiction: schedule failover drills (tabletop first, then live), measure actual RTO against the objective, and fix the gaps the drill exposes. The drill report is the DR plan's proof.
Drill types: tabletop (walkthrough, cheap, finds process gaps), partial failover (one tier, tests mechanics), full failover (the real thing, needs a maintenance window). Escalate through the types.
Common drill findings: missing runbook steps, stale credentials, DNS TTLs too long, data lag beyond RPO. Each finding updates the plan — the plan improves because the drill exists.
Game days: surprise drills that test the team, not just the tech. Who gets paged, who decides, who communicates — the human failover path matters as much as the technical one.

example.code: Drill report: planned RTO 30min, actual 55min — gaps: DNS TTL 1h (fix: 60s), runbook missing LB step (fix: update). Next drill in 90 days.
example.walkthrough: The drill measures reality; the report fixes the plan.

pitfalls: Findings not fed back into the plan.

lessons.title: Backup Security: Ransomware Considerations
concepts: Backups are the ransomware recovery path — which makes them the attacker's secondary target. Immutable/object-lock backups can't be encrypted by the attacker; air-gapped copies can't be reached.
OCI controls: object retention rules (WORM), cross-region copies (attacker in region A can't easily reach region B's vault), separate-compartment backup storage with restricted IAM.
IAM for backups: backup-writing principals can't delete (separate delete permissions, MFA for deletion). The ransomware can't encrypt what it can't delete or overwrite.
Test restores prove recoverability; restore drills prove speed. The ransomware tabletop asks: 'backups intact?' and 'how fast is the restore?' — answer both before the incident.

example.code: oci os object retention-rule create --bucket-name backups --display-name ransomware-lock --duration '{"time-amount":30,"time-unit":"DAYS"}'
example.walkthrough: 30-day retention rule — backups the attacker can't purge.

pitfalls: Deletable backups in the same compartment.
No retention rules on backup buckets.

lessons.title: Exam Blueprint and Weighting
concepts: The Architect Associate blueprint weights roughly: IAM/security, networking, compute, storage/database, observability, pricing/governance. Allocate study hours proportionally — networking + IAM deserve the most.
Question styles: single-best-answer (most), multiple-select (read the count!), and scenario stems (2-3 sentences setting constraints). The stem's constraints eliminate options — read them first.
'Most cost-effective', 'with minimal operational overhead', 'meets security requirements' — the qualifiers in the stem are the selection criteria. Underline them mentally before reading options.

Wrong-option patterns: over-engineered (multi-region for AD failure), insecure (public DB), mismatched service (HeatWave for OLTP), and the 'almost right' (one constraint violated). Learn to spot the violated constraint.

example.code: Stem dissection: 'spiky web traffic, minimal ops, cost-sensitive' -> constraints: elastic, managed, cheap. Options violating any constraint die first.
example.walkthrough: Constraints first, options second — always.

pitfalls: Reading options before the stem's constraints.
lessons.try_it: Dissect 10 stems into constraints

lessons.title: High-Yield: Networking Questions
concepts: Top networking patterns: public/private subnets with IGW/NAT; NSG tier matrix; LB with health checks; peering with non-overlapping CIDRs; DRG for hybrid. Five patterns cover most questions.
Gateway selection: internet access for public -> IGW; private outbound -> NAT; OCI services privately -> service gateway; on-prem -> DRG + VPN/FastConnect. Requirement -> gateway is mechanical.
Security lists vs NSGs: subnet-level vs instance-level; the exam's tier-isolation questions want NSGs. Stateful default; stateless needs return rules — a favorite trap.
Peering traps: overlapping CIDRs (impossible), transitive assumption (false), missing return routes. Check all three on any peering question.

example.code: Flash pattern: 'private instances need OS patches, no internet' -> NAT gateway (outbound) or service gateway (OCI services). Two options, both valid, context decides.
example.walkthrough: Five patterns, drilled to reflex.

lessons.try_it: Drill gateway selection: 15 requirements

lessons.title: High-Yield: IAM and Security Questions
concepts: Policy syntax: Allow group X to <verb> <resource> in compartment Y [where ...]. The exam shows policies and asks what they allow — parse the sentence mechanically.
Verb hierarchy: inspect < read < use < manage. 'Can the group launch instances?' needs use/manage on instances — read is insufficient. Verb questions are free marks if you know the ladder.
Dynamic groups + instance principals: instances accessing OCI services without stored credentials. 'Application on instance needs bucket access' -> dynamic group + policy, never API keys.
Cloud Guard vs Security Zones vs Vault: monitor vs prevent vs secrets. 'Block public buckets at creation' -> zones; 'detect misconfigurations' -> guard; 'store passwords' -> vault.

example.code: Policy parse: 'Allow group auditors to inspect instances in compartment prod' -> can list/describe, cannot start/stop (needs use), cannot create (needs manage).
example.walkthrough: Parse policies like sentences — the verbs decide.

lessons.try_it: Parse 10 policies into allowed/denied

lessons.title: High-Yield: Compute, Storage, Database
concepts: Compute: shape-to-workload (flex default, GPU for ML, burstable for idle, preemptible for batch); pool + autoscaling + LB for elastic web; custom images for consistency. Workload profile -> choice.
Storage: block for instance disks, object for blobs/static, FSS for shared POSIX. Performance tiers on block; lifecycle tiers on object. The three-way choice appears constantly.
Database: ATP (OLTP autonomous), ADW (warehouse), HeatWave (MySQL analytics), NoSQL (key-value), DB Systems (managed control). Workload shape -> service, mechanically.
Cross-cutting: 'minimal operational overhead' pushes to managed/autonomous/serverless across all three. The qualifier appears in half the questions — let it decide.

example.code: Qualifier drill: 'minimal ops' -> Autonomous over DB Systems, Container Instances over OKE, serverless where offered. One qualifier, consistent direction.
example.walkthrough: 'Minimal ops' is a compass — follow it.

pitfalls: Object storage for shared file locking.
lessons.try_it: Build the compute/storage/DB chooser table

lessons.title: Triage and Time Management
concepts: 65-70% to pass (varies by form); ~60 questions in ~90 minutes — about 90 seconds per question. Budget: 60s easy, 2min hard, flag beyond that. The clock is the real opponent.
First pass: answer what you know, flag the rest. Second pass: flagged questions with remaining time. Never leave blanks — no penalty for wrong answers, so educated guesses on everything.
Flag triggers: 40-line configs, 'select THREE' with similar options, and any question you've re-read twice. Flagging is discipline, not surrender.
Final 10 minutes: review flagged, then guess remaining. A guessed answer has 25% expected value; a blank has 0%. The math is unambiguous.

example.code: Time plan: 60 questions, 90 min -> 45 min first pass (45s/q), 30 min flagged, 15 min review+guess. Write it on the scratch paper first.
example.walkthrough: Write the time plan before question one.

lessons.title: Final Review: The One-Page Cheatsheet
concepts: Build the one-pager: per service — use case, key limit, pricing axis, and the X-vs-Y rule. One page, dense, personal. Writing it IS the review.

Constraint -> answer mappings: 'survive AD failure' -> multi-AD; 'survive region failure' -> multi-region + replication; 'minimal ops' -> managed/autonomous; 'cheapest' -> preemptible/burstable/Always Free.

Trap checklist: public DB (flag it), overlapping CIDRs (impossible), ROWNUM-like ordering traps in OCI? No — but 'select TWO' counts, verb ladders, and gateway mismatches. Your trap list, reviewed nightly.
Exam day: sleep, arrive early, stem-first reading, flag discipline, guess everything. You've done the work — the exam is just the demonstration.

example.code: One-pager excerpt: 'NAT: private->internet outbound only. Service GW: private->OCI services. IGW: public<->internet. DRG: hybrid + remote peering.'
example.walkthrough: The one-pager is the exam in miniature.

pitfalls: Cramming new topics the night before.

simulations.brief: A new instance in the Frankfurt region cannot reach an instance in Ashburn, but instances inside each region talk fine. The network team suspects the cross-region path.
simulations.debrief: Cross-region traffic in OCI rides a remote peering connection between DRGs with matching route rules on both sides. When intra-region works but cross-region fails, the RPC or one side's route table is the suspect — not the security lists inside each VCN.

evidence: Frankfurt VM -> Ashburn VM: 100% packet loss. Frankfurt VM -> Frankfurt VM: OK
Each region has its own VCN with a DRG attached
steps.explain: Same-region traffic works, so the VCNs, subnets, and security lists are healthy. The failure is specific to the cross-region path, which in OCI means the remote peering connection (RPC) between the two DRGs — or the route rules pointing at it.
options: Add an ingress rule to the Frankfurt security list
Check the remote peering connection between the DRGs and the route rules on both sides
steps.symptom: Cross-region ping fails; same-region ping works.

evidence: Frankfurt DRG: RPC status PEERED. Ashburn DRG: no RPC attachment
Frankfurt route table has a rule for 10.1.0.0/16 via the RPC; Ashburn has no route back
steps.explain: Peering is one-sided: Frankfurt peers out, but Ashburn has no RPC attachment and no return route. Remote peering requires the RPC on both DRGs and route rules on both sides — fix by creating the Ashburn-side RPC and adding the return route.
options: Delete and recreate the Frankfurt VCN
Create the RPC attachment on the Ashburn DRG and add the return route rule
Open all ports in both security lists
Move both instances to the same AD
steps.symptom: RPC exists only on the Frankfurt side; no return route.
